post.summary: Send one treatment’s ДНЕВНИК to Google Drive
post.description:
The same Приложение 1 document the `GET` of this path returns as bytes, put in the farm’s connected Google Drive instead. Answers JSON saying where it landed, so a client can link straight to the file.

**No request body.** The handle is this document’s only input and it is a path segment — iOS writes the full URL including the query string to the device log, unsuppressably.

**Administrators only**, and that is not a separate rule: the export needs the tenant-wide Google credential, and resolving it decrypts and may rotate a stored secret. So a farm worker who recorded the treatment can DOWNLOAD this document and cannot export it — a real cost, accepted deliberately rather than inventing a permission for “may send this farm’s documents to an account the admin connected”.

Exports accumulate in one folder the app creates, addressed by an id stored on the connection. That id can outlive the folder: `drive.file` only sees files this app created, so a farmer deleting or binning it is invisible until the next export. Both are treated as ordinary states and a new folder is made — `folderCreated` says so, which is what lets a client explain an apparently empty folder.

Behind the `integrations.google` flag and the `JOURNAL` module. Node runtime, 60s budget.

200.description: Exported. The file id, its name in Drive, and Google’s link.

400.description:
`GOOGLE_NOT_CONNECTED` — no Google account is connected for this farm. An administrator connects one in Settings → Integrations.

`GOOGLE_DRIVE_NOT_GRANTED` — connected, but Drive was never granted. Google’s consent screen lets the scopes be ticked individually, so this is an ordinary state rather than a corrupt one, and it is refused BEFORE the document is rendered. The fix is to reconnect and grant Drive.

`GOOGLE_GRANT_REVOKED` — the stored refresh token no longer works. The server already refreshes an expired access token before trying, so a 401 from Google after that means the grant itself was withdrawn, which only reconnecting fixes.

`GOOGLE_DRIVE_REFUSED` — Google refused the write for its own reasons, most often a full Drive. Distinguished from `GOOGLE_DRIVE_NOT_GRANTED` deliberately: both arrive as a 403, and telling a farmer to reconnect when their storage is full would be wrong advice confidently given.

`GOOGLE_DRIVE_RATE_LIMITED` — Google is rate-limiting requests; retry shortly. A THIRD code rather than a second meaning for `GOOGLE_DRIVE_REFUSED`, whose sentence tells the operator to check their Drive storage — right for the 403 quota case and wrong advice for a 429, which is the same trap one line up pointing the other way. Before #2447 a 429 fell through to a 502, and because `expose` is `status < 500` the message was replaced by a bare "An error occurred" with no remedy at all.

Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

post.description:
ONE route, TWO request content types, and which one you send decides what happens:

**`multipart/form-data`** uploads the file, mints the FileRecord through the shared storage pipeline and links it — this is the photo-logging path from the field.

**`application/json`** attaches an ALREADY-uploaded FileRecord by id (`{ fileRecordId, caption? }`). Upload first, here or via `/evidence/uploads`, then reference the id.

Re-attaching a file that is already linked returns the EXISTING link rather than creating a second one, so a retry after a dropped connection does not double-attach a photo.

**An uploaded image is re-encoded before it is stored** (#1812). EXIF, XMP and GPS are dropped, which on this route is the point rather than a side effect: a journal attachment is a photo taken at the operation it records, so its GPS tag is by construction the parcel being worked. The format is preserved — a JPEG is stored as a JPEG — and the pixels are unchanged; only the metadata goes. Orientation is baked in first, so a portrait photo from a phone is stored upright rather than relying on a tag that is about to be removed.

**Refusal codes.** This route validates the upload itself rather than going through `ingestUploadedFile`, so these are the ones it raises:
- `IMAGE_UNREADABLE` — the magic number said this was an image and the decoder disagreed, so the container is truncated or malformed. A different photo, not the same one re-exported. Raised in place of storing the bytes unstripped, because a file that cannot be decoded is also one no viewer in the product could render.
- `FILE_TYPE_NOT_ALLOWED` — the type is outside the shared allowlist. Checked on the DECLARED type first and again on the sniffed one, so bytes whose real content is inadmissible are refused even when the claim passed.
- `FILE_TOO_LARGE` — over the shared maximum. The limit is on the wire as `maxBytes` rather than only in the sentence, so a translated message can still name the figure.
- `INVALID_FILE` — the `multipart/form-data` body carried no usable file part.
- `PDF_UNREADABLE` — the bytes sniffed as a PDF and could not be parsed, rewritten or re-serialised, so its document metadata (`/Author`, `/Producer`, `/CreationDate` and the XMP packet) could not be removed (#2035). Refused rather than stored unstripped, for the same reason as `IMAGE_UNREADABLE` above: a privacy property that degrades silently to no privacy is not one. Raised on every surface that stores an uploaded PDF — this route, the evidence upload, and the cost-entry invoice through `ingestUploadedFile`.

Note what this route does NOT raise: `UPLOAD_INFECTED` and `UPLOAD_SCANNER_UNAVAILABLE` are thrown by `scanOrRefuse`, and this path uses `scanUploadedBuffer`, which RETURNS a verdict instead. An infected attachment is therefore stored with `scanStatus: INFECTED` and refused by the download gate rather than refused at upload.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user.   Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. - `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

get.description: FARM_TASK + FIELD_OPERATION rows, soonest-due first (null `dueAt` sinks to the bottom, newest `createdAt` breaks ties), capped at 200 AFTER the merge — so a tenant with more than 200 open jobs sees a truncated queue with no marker saying so. Carries a weak ETag and honours `If-None-Match` with a 304, which is what makes a focus-revalidate cheap on rural LTE.

schema.description: Comma-separated WorkItemStatus members: OPEN, TRIAGED, IN_PROGRESS, BLOCKED, PENDING_REVIEW, RESOLVED, CLOSED, CANCELED. An unknown member is a 400 for the WHOLE request — a filter that silently drops a member would widen the result set past what the operator asked for.

schema.description: Only the caller’s OUTSTANDING work — OPEN/TRIAGED/IN_PROGRESS/BLOCKED. Drops PENDING_REVIEW as well as the terminal statuses: a field operation whose parcels are all marked is the reviewer’s turn, not the operator’s. It is a PRESENCE flag once it validates — the handler tests `!== undefined`, not the value — but only `1` and `true` validate; anything else is a 400, so there is no way to send `open=0` and mean "off". Omit it instead.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not modify records. Params: `role`. It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. 404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

post.description: Send `Idempotency-Key` ALWAYS, minted BEFORE the first attempt and reused on every retry of the same logical write — the outbox uses its queue-item id. The server stores it as `clientMutationId` under a unique (tenantId, clientMutationId) index, scoped to `type: FARM_TASK`, and returns the ORIGINAL task on a replay. Without the header a re-send over flaky LTE mints a SECOND task, and creation is not just a row: it also writes an audit event, emits TASK_CREATED and enqueues an assignee notification, all of which would fire twice.

201.description: The created Task — the FULL row, wider than a list item, with `assignee` and `createdBy` resolved. On an idempotent replay this is the ORIGINAL task, still 201, but read back WITHOUT those two includes — treat both as optional rather than assuming the shape of the first response.

patch.summary: Mark one prescription line DONE / SKIPPED / PENDING

The write the offline outbox replays, so treat `If-Match: <version>` (digits only) as mandatory: it is what stops a queued mark clobbering a supervisor’s later edit. An absent or non-integer `If-Match` SKIPS the version check entirely — a silent last-write-wins, not an error.

A stale version has TWO possible answers, and telling them apart is the point. If the line already carries the status this write wanted, the intent is satisfied: 200 with `alreadyApplied: true`, the current `version`, and `resolved: false`. Otherwise 409 `STALE_DATA`. Answering a replay of the operator’s own success with a 409 asks them to resolve keep-mine versus take-server against themselves, which is not a question anyone can answer.

Authorisation is unusual here: the ASSIGNED operator may mark their own job even without general write permission. PATCH is the only method — there is no PUT alias, and no way to add a line to an existing job.

It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

get.description: Returns a FLAT ARRAY by default. Send `limit` or `cursor` and the SAME operation returns `{ items, pageInfo }` instead — a client must branch on the query it sent. Both shapes carry a weak ETag and honour `If-None-Match` with a 304.

schema.description: Sending `limit` OR `cursor` switches the response to the paginated envelope.

parameters.description: Sending `limit` OR `cursor` switches the response to the paginated envelope.
parameters.name: limit

schema.description: ACTIVE or ARCHIVED.

parameters.description: ACTIVE or ARCHIVED.
parameters.name: status

schema.description: Free-text search.

parameters.description: Free-text search.
parameters.name: q

schema.description: Comma-separated LocationKind members, e.g. `BIN,STORAGE`. A Location is a field or a storage row depending on kind, so an unfiltered list MIXES growing areas with grain bins. Values that are not real enum members are dropped rather than rejected.

parameters.name: kind

200.description: An array of locations, or the paginated envelope (see description).

304.description: Not Modified — the payload still matches the client’s `If-None-Match`.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

Split on a parameter rather than returned together because the caller shows ONE crop at a time: a single response carrying every crop’s geometry would be large for a client that discards all but one group.

**This is the farm-wide read that `GET /locations/{id}/parcels` is not.** That one answers "what is in this block" and carries soil, ownership and lease state; this one answers "where on the farm is this crop" and carries the block name instead. Before it existed a client had to fan out one request per block and group them itself.

**Matching on `crop` is case-insensitive and trimmed.** `Parcel.cropType` is a free string that an import stamps, so stored rows can disagree about case among themselves; a value round-tripped from the crop list resolves regardless.

Parcels with no crop appear in NEITHER answer. "No crop" does not answer "which crop did you treat", and such a parcel is still reachable through the per-block list.

Order is `name`, then `id`. The id tiebreak is contractual (#1391): parcel names are not unique, so without it a capped read could return a different subset between requests with nothing changed.

parameters.description: A crop value as returned by this same operation without the parameter. Omit for the crop list. Case-insensitive, trimmed; blank is treated as omitted.

404.description:

post.description:
This is where a field operation is created — there is no POST under `/field-operations`. Exactly ONE input: a product OR a fertilizer, never both and never neither, and the chosen kind’s dose and unit are then required.

Send `Idempotency-Key` — the outbox replays a queued job with its item id, and the usecase returns the original instead of a duplicate. The replay check requires `parcelCount > 0` on the existing job, because the create spans TWO transactions and a crash between them leaves a Task with no lines that must NOT be reported as synced.

**400 codes for the input a job applies.** `OPERATION_INPUT_AMBIGUOUS` — not exactly one kind, or an id AND a name for the same kind. `PRODUCT_DOSE_REQUIRED` / `FERTILIZER_DOSE_REQUIRED` — the chosen kind needs its dose and unit. `PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND` / `FERTILIZER_NOT_FOUND` — the id names nothing in this farm. `FERTILIZER_EXPECTED` — the fertiliser field was given an item that is not a `FERTILIZER`. **The converse is deliberately NOT enforced**: a liquid fertiliser applied through a sprayer is a legitimate SPRAY, so the product field accepts any category — see `productItemId`, whose own description claimed the opposite until #2362. `SEED_EXPECTED` — `operationType` is `SEED` and the item is not a `SEED`. The ONE exception to that permissiveness, and it is about the kind rather than the field: #2316 excludes сеитба from the БАБХ register, so without the lock a real plant-protection product recorded as a sowing would leave the regulated document. It was missing from this list because the code is documented on the journal treatments route and `error-codes-are-documented` asks whether a code is named ANYWHERE, not whether it is named on the operations that raise it. `PRODUCT_NAME_REQUIRED` — a `productName` empty once trimmed and sanitised. `PESTICIDE_REGULATORY_FIELDS_REQUIRED` — a typed name has to CREATE a plant protection product and `newProductRegistration` is missing a field, named in `params.missing`. `DOSE_UNIT_HAS_NO_BASE` — a typed name has to create a product but the dose unit is not a `<base>-per-<area>` rate, so no stock unit can be derived; create the product from the catalogue instead. `ACTIVITY_APPLIES_NO_INPUT` — a product or fertiliser was sent with an `operationType` of `PRUNE`, `CULTIVATE` or `HARVEST`, which apply nothing (#2316); refused rather than dropped, because silently ignoring it would file a spraying as a pruning in a regulated record. **This operation cannot raise it**: its `operationType` enum admits only the four input-applying kinds, so the refusal is defence in depth behind the usecase — named here so a client switching on codes finds it in the spec either way. (That sentence used to end “until the activities route ships”. The activities route shipped in #2344, and this enum still admits only the four, so the statement is now permanent rather than pending.)

post.description:
ONE 200 with TWO media types, chosen by the `save` flag in the body. Default (`save` absent or false) → `application/pdf` bytes with `Content-Disposition: attachment`. `save: true` → `application/json` `{ fileRecordId, fileName }`, with the PDF filed in the register instead. Negotiate on what you SENT; an `Accept` header has no effect.

Read-only data, authorised by `assertCanRead` inside the generator. Runs on the Node runtime with a 60s budget.

**A block with nothing recorded in the period gets NO document** (#2183, owner ruling 2026-10-23). It answers `404 REGISTER_EMPTY_FOR_PERIOD`, and a client should render that as "nothing was recorded for this period" rather than as an error — it is the ordinary outcome for an untreated block, not a fault. This reverses the previous behaviour, which printed the blank form like the paper original; both options were put to the owner and the blank form was declined twice.

Within a document that DOES have content, a data section with no rows is left out entirely. The sampling and ОДБХ inspector sheets are NOT data sections — they are ruled forms that arrive blank for completion by hand — so they are always present.

Either the block does not exist, or it exists and had a quiet period.

post.summary: Send a block’s ДНЕВНИК to Google Drive
post.description:
The same document the `POST` of this path returns as bytes, put in the farm’s connected Google Drive instead. Answers JSON saying where it landed.

**A separate path rather than a third value on that route’s `save`.** That flag is already a media-type switch — `application/pdf` bytes or `application/json` — and its own schema documents it as a trap. A third destination decided by a body field would compound that rather than follow it.

**Administrators only**, unlike the download, which a writer can produce. Not a separate rule: the export needs the tenant-wide Google credential, and resolving it decrypts and may rotate a stored secret.

Exports accumulate in one folder the app creates, addressed by an id stored on the connection. That id can outlive the folder — `drive.file` only sees files this app created, so a farmer deleting or binning it is invisible until the next export. Both are ordinary states and a new folder is made; `folderCreated` says so.

Behind the `integrations.google` flag and the `JOURNAL` module. Node runtime, 60s budget.

schema.description: Location id.

parameters.description: Location id.
parameters.name: id

200.description: Exported. The file id, its name in Drive, and Google’s link.

400.description:
`GOOGLE_NOT_CONNECTED` — no Google account is connected for this farm. An administrator connects one in Settings → Integrations.

`GOOGLE_DRIVE_NOT_GRANTED` — connected, but Drive was never granted. Google’s consent screen lets the scopes be ticked individually, so this is an ordinary state rather than a corrupt one, and it is refused BEFORE the document is rendered. The fix is to reconnect and grant Drive.

`GOOGLE_GRANT_REVOKED` — the stored refresh token no longer works. The server already refreshes an expired access token before trying, so a 401 from Google after that means the grant itself was withdrawn, which only reconnecting fixes.

`GOOGLE_DRIVE_REFUSED` — Google refused the write for its own reasons, most often a full Drive. Distinguished from `GOOGLE_DRIVE_NOT_GRANTED` deliberately: both arrive as a 403, and telling a farmer to reconnect when their storage is full would be wrong advice confidently given.

`GOOGLE_DRIVE_RATE_LIMITED` — Google is rate-limiting requests; retry shortly. A THIRD code rather than a second meaning for `GOOGLE_DRIVE_REFUSED`, whose sentence tells the operator to check their Drive storage — right for the 403 quota case and wrong advice for a 429, which is the same trap one line up pointing the other way. Before #2447 a 429 fell through to a 502, and because `expose` is `status < 500` the message was replaced by a bare "An error occurred" with no remedy at all.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. - `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description: Unknown job, or one belonging to another tenant or location — deliberately indistinguishable. BARE `{ error }` body.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

post.description:
multipart/form-data. The parse NEVER runs on the request thread — the handler validates the extension, enforces the per-format byte cap on `file.size` before buffering anything, stages the bytes and queues the job. The worker REPLACES the location’s parcels, so nothing has changed yet when this returns; poll `getSpatialImportJob` first.

Every failure answers the canonical `ErrorResponse` envelope with a code (#1447). It did NOT until then: it answered a bare `{ error: "<sentence>" }`, and with no code to translate by a native client passed the English sentence through to a Bulgarian screen. Switch on `error.code`; `message` is only the fallback for a code you do not recognise.

400.description: Missing, non-file, or empty upload. `error.code` is `FILE_REQUIRED` when no file part was sent and `FILE_EMPTY` when one was sent with no bytes — a different fix for the person uploading, which is why they are two codes.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

413.description: Over the per-format byte cap. `error.code` is `SPATIAL_UPLOAD_TOO_LARGE`, with `params.sizeBytes`, `params.limitBytes` and `params.format`. The caps differ per format (5 MB shapefile, 10 MB KML·GeoJSON), so the limit TRAVELS rather than being restated by each client. Raw integer bytes and not the «5.0 MB» the message uses: that string carries an English decimal point, and a client writing «7,2 MB» would have had to parse it back out (#1447).

415.description: Unsupported extension. `error.code` is `UNSUPPORTED_FILE_TYPE`, with the accepted extensions in `params.allowed` so a client can list them in its own language.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

get.description: On completion `result.details` carries parcelCount / format / bounds; on failure `failedCode` + `failedParams` carry the complexity, topology or CRS refusal in a form you can translate, and `failedReason` keeps the English sentence as the fallback. See `ImportJobStatus.failedCode` for the codes this poll can send.

post.summary: Bring the farm’s Google Calendar into line with its deadlines
post.description:
Writes the farm’s dated work — task due dates, lease expiry, contract delivery windows, planting cycles, support-scheme deadlines and the rest of the nine calendar sources — into a separate «Agrent — Срокове» calendar in the connected Google account.

A **sync**, not a push: the desired set is computed, the calendar is read back, and the difference is applied. Task due dates and lease expiry move, so a push would leave the farmer planning around dates that no longer exist.

**Safe to repeat.** A second call finds every event already matching and reports it as `unchanged` — a property of the diff, so no idempotency key is involved.

**Two things it deliberately will not do, and both are reported rather than hidden:**

| situation | what happens | field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the source read was truncated | nothing is deleted | `partial: true` |
| the farmer edited one of our events | it is neither updated nor deleted | `skippedEdited` |

In both cases an absence from the desired set is not evidence that the farm no longer wants the event, and a sync that deleted on it would destroy real information. Events outside the sync’s own window — 30 days back, a year forward — are left alone for the same reason, which is what stops a rolling window from erasing the farm’s history.

Administrator only, and behind the `integrations.google` flag. The credential is a tenant-wide secret, so the sync cannot be more open than the token resolver that decrypts it.

400.description: `GOOGLE_NOT_CONNECTED` — no Google account is connected for this farm. `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_NOT_GRANTED` — a connection exists but Calendar was not granted, which is an ordinary state because Google’s consent screen lets the scopes be ticked individually; the remedy is to reconnect and grant Calendar. `GOOGLE_GRANT_REVOKED` — the stored grant is no longer authorised. `GOOGLE_CALENDAR_REFUSED` — Google refused the write for some other reason, a rate limit among them; retry shortly rather than reconnecting a connection that is fine.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

Each carries a `message`. - `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. get.description:
A 256² Web Mercator JPEG from the newest flight year whose coverage polygon includes the tile. Signed-in only, so this is not an open proxy onto a government service, and the upstream URL never reaches the client.

**Three answers, and the difference between two of them is a contract:**

| status | meaning | what a client should do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `200` `image/jpeg` | imagery | draw it |
| `204` | no imagery here, and that is FINAL | draw plain ground; safe to remember |
| `503` | the server could not find out | draw ground and ASK AGAIN later |

A 204 means the Ministry has not photographed this — no covering flight year, or the source’s blank tile. It is safe to cache for a session. A 503 means an upstream failure and must NOT be remembered: caching it would show bare ground over land that is photographed until the client restarts.

`X-Ortho-Year` names the flight year the pixels came from, so a client need not ask `/ortho/coverage` again to label them.

**No `ETag`, deliberately.** `Cache-Control: immutable` gets the caching benefit without a conditional round-trip, and an `ETag` invites `If-None-Match` — a 304 that a client without a 304 branch would read as "not an image" and draw as ground, which is the same silent blank the 204/503 split exists to prevent.

Zoom is clamped to 10-19: 25 cm native resolution means the source has nothing beyond z19, and below z10 one tile fans across the whole country. Behind the `agro.orthophoto` flag AND an operator-set upstream; either absent answers 404.

**On the documented `429`: no rate limit applies to this route for a session or bearer caller, and a client should not build backoff for one.** That status is boilerplate — all 273 operations in this document carry it. The `/api/t/` limiter in middleware is gated on API-key auth AND on the request presenting an `iflk_` bearer; a cookie session or a native JWE bearer falls through untouched, and no tile route carries a limiter of its own.

That is deliberate rather than an oversight. A map asks for every visible tile at once — 15-20 on a cold screen, another burst per pan — so a per-user budget sized for ordinary API traffic would throttle the map into a retry loop, which is worse than no budget. What actually needs protecting is the МЗХ service, and that is bounded server-side at four concurrent upstream requests regardless of how many clients ask; a cache hit costs this server almost nothing.
