get.description:
The footer under «Ортофотокарта»: «Ортофото: МЗХ, заснемане <date>».

Resolved ONCE per area rather than per tile, which is why it is its own endpoint: the source serves each year as a separate layer, stacking them in one request returns blank, and probing year-by-year per tile would mean up to six upstream requests for every tile of a cold pan.

`year: null` is an ordinary answer. Each year’s flight covers roughly a third of the country, and an area outside Bulgaria answers null without the Ministry being asked at all.

Behind the `agro.orthophoto` flag AND an operator-set upstream.

schema.description: `minLon,minLat,maxLon,maxLat` — LONGITUDE first, the GeoJSON order. Refused above 0.5° on either axis, so one request cannot sweep the country.

parameters.description: `minLon,minLat,maxLon,maxLat` — LONGITUDE first, the GeoJSON order. Refused above 0.5° on either axis, so one request cannot sweep the country.
parameters.name: bbox

200.description: The newest covering year and its flight date.

400.description: `ORTHO_BBOX_INVALID` — the `bbox` is malformed, out of range, inverted, or wider than 0.5° on an axis. One code for all of them: every one is a client bug rather than something a farmer can act on, and the message says which. A well-formed box OUTSIDE Bulgaria is not an error — it answers `year: null`, because panning too far is not a mistake.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

THREE PERMISSION codes are described here, and they are the most diffuse of all of them — 106, 51 and 1 call sites respectively, under most mutating and administrative operations in this document:

- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not modify records. Params: `role`. It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

get.description:
GeoJSON in EPSG:4326, drawn as thin labelled outlines under the farm’s own parcels. `properties.id` is the Ministry’s `PHBIDENT`, which is what a farmer matches against a Ministry document.

The server caps the list at its own number regardless of the area asked for, and `truncated` says when it did. A client should still bound its own requests — but a cap that lives only in the client is not a cap.

A feature arriving without `PHBIDENT` is DROPPED rather than returned unlabelled: an outline a farmer cannot match to a document is worse than one fewer outline.

Behind the `agro.orthophoto` flag AND an operator-set upstream.

get.description: The whole calculator payload, identical to what the web page renders — both call `buildCalculatorPayload` in `@/lib/grain/calculator-payload`, which is the contract. Top level: `generatedAt`, `seasonId`, `rows`, `farm`, `exclusions`, `unvalued`, `cashOut`, `unallocatedToCrop`, `imputedLandCharge`, `truncated`. Every field is a number, string, boolean or array thereof — no Decimal, no Date. `unallocatedToCrop` and `imputedLandCharge` sit BESIDE the cost side and must never be folded into a cost line: a spread is conserved across `rows + unallocatedToCrop`, so summing only the rows reports a cost that shrank. Carries a weak ETag and honours `If-None-Match` with a 304. Requires the GRAIN module; a tenant without it gets 403 `module_disabled: GRAIN`.

200.description: The calculator payload (see description for the top-level shape).

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

post.description:
Creates one cost entry. `allocationBasis` decides how it reaches a crop — read the enum's own docs before choosing, because the basis is what makes a cost attributable rather than stranded in `unallocatedToCrop` on the calculator.

**Honours `Idempotency-Key`.** Send one, minted BEFORE the first attempt and reused on every retry of the same logical write. The server maps it to `clientMutationId` and a replay returns the ORIGINAL row rather than booking the figure twice. These are FINANCIAL records: an undeduped retry moves net worth with nothing erroring.

**The salary breakdown is both-or-neither, and `PAYROLL` only.** `payrollHeadcount` and `payrollAnnualPerPerson` record how a salary figure was arrived at — «брой хора × годишна заплата» — so the form can show the breakdown and a defaults read can recall it. `amount` stays authoritative and is deliberately NOT cross-checked against the product: a farm whose third hire started in May will enter a total below `headcount × perPerson`, and refusing that would block a true figure to protect an identity nobody asked for. Sending one without the other is `PAYROLL_BREAKDOWN_INCOMPLETE`, with the absent field named in `params.missing`; sending either on a non-PAYROLL category is `PAYROLL_BREAKDOWN_NOT_APPLICABLE`.

**`allocationBasis: CROP` scopes the whole cost to ONE crop** (#1530) and is the farmer’s own per-crop figure rather than a spread across land. It requires `commodityCanonical` — any spelling the crop vocabulary resolves, stored canonical, so `Canola` is persisted as `rapeseed`. A commodity the vocabulary does not cover is REFUSED rather than stored as null: such a row has no commodity to sum onto and would be accepted, listed, and absent from every figure. 

Three refusals carry codes. `CROP_COST_NEEDS_COMMODITY` — basis `CROP` with no crop named. `COMMODITY_NOT_APPLICABLE` — a crop named on any other basis, with the basis in `params.basis`; refused rather than ignored because a crop left on a row whose basis later returns to `CROP` would start carrying the cost with nobody having chosen it. `CROP_COST_HAS_SPATIAL_LINK` — a `CROP` entry also linking a planting, parcel or location, with the offending fields in `params.links`; such an entry answers “which crop”, not “which land”, so a place link would store an instruction the allocator ignores. 

A `CROP` cost **supersedes** the consumption-derived cost for its (commodity, season) rather than adding to it — the farmer’s figure wins, and the season is the one containing `incurredOn`, else its calendar year. So it is a fourth slice of `cashCostTotal` on the calculator, never a second count of the same crop-year.

Eleven more refusals carry codes, and all of them are 400s.

**The link** — `COST_ENTRY_MULTIPLE_DOMAIN_LINKS` (more than one of the domain links set, count in `params.chosen`); `COST_ENTRY_LEASE_REQUIRES_RENT` (`leaseId` on a non-RENT category); `COST_ENTRY_PARCELS_REQUIRE_SUBSET_BASIS` (`allocationParcelIds` on a basis other than `PARCEL_SUBSET`).

**The basis** — `COST_ENTRY_BASIS_CONFLICTS_WITH_SPATIAL_LINK` (a basis that spreads across land of its own, also linking a place; the basis is in `params.basis`); `COST_ENTRY_PARCEL_SUBSET_NEEDS_TWO` (a `PARCEL_SUBSET` naming fewer than two distinct parcels — one parcel is a `parcelId` link, not a subset).

**The references** — `REFERENCE_NOT_IN_TENANT` covers every one of them, with which reference in `params.reference`: the six single links (`planting`, `season`, `location`, `parcel`, `lease`, `item`) and, as `parcels`, the `PARCEL_SUBSET` set. It is ONE code across the whole API rather than one per surface, so a client handles this refusal once. It answers **400 rather than 404 deliberately**: a 404 would confirm the row exists in SOME tenant, which is what a cross-tenant probe is for. The reference TYPE is returned; the id is not.

**The invoice** — `COST_ENTRY_INVOICE_FILE_NOT_FOUND`, `COST_ENTRY_INVOICE_UPLOAD_INCOMPLETE` (the upload never finished) and `COST_ENTRY_INVOICE_FILE_DELETED`.

**The date** — `COST_ENTRY_INVALID_DATE`, with the field named in `params.field`.

**The currency** — `COST_ENTRY_CURRENCY_NOT_EUR`, with the submitted code in `params.currency`. Costs are recorded in euro: every euro spelling the old free-text field produced is accepted (`EUR`, `EURO`, `EUROS`, `€`, `E`), and anything else is refused. Lev is refused too, which is the non-obvious part — the cost calculator CONVERTS lev at the fixed 1.95583 peg when totalling, so a lev row reads correctly on the calculator while being unsavable here. Those are deliberately different questions: “can this be totalled in euro” and “may this be stored”.

post.summary: Record a whole cost sheet, all-or-nothing

Creates up to 25 cost entries in ONE transaction. Either every line is booked or none is — a half-saved sheet is worse than one that failed, because the farmer cannot tell which lines landed. Each line is exactly the `POST /grain/costs` body, so every rule documented there applies per line, including the `CROP` basis refusals and the salary breakdown.

**`lines` must contain at least one entry.** An empty batch is refused rather than absorbed as a no-op: a 201 for a write that did nothing is what makes an offline outbox believe it has synced and drop the sheet.

**A line that violates any rule refuses the WHOLE sheet, before anything is written.** Every line is validated up front, so the batch cannot book six rows and then discover line 7 carries a contradictory allocation basis.

**Honours `Idempotency-Key`, and it is the SHEET’s key.** Send one minted before the first attempt and reused on every retry of the same sheet. Note the server derives a per-line key from it internally — `CostEntry` carries a unique index on `(tenantId, clientMutationId)`, so the lines cannot literally share your key — and a replay returns the ORIGINAL rows, in the order you sent them, rather than booking the sheet twice. Do not construct or depend on the derived form; it is an implementation detail and is deliberately not read back by prefix.

The 25-line bound is not politeness: the sheet is one interactive transaction, and an unbounded batch is a transaction whose size the client chooses.

Eleven more refusals carry codes, and all of them are 400s.

**The link** — `COST_ENTRY_MULTIPLE_DOMAIN_LINKS` (more than one of the domain links set, count in `params.chosen`); `COST_ENTRY_LEASE_REQUIRES_RENT` (`leaseId` on a non-RENT category); `COST_ENTRY_PARCELS_REQUIRE_SUBSET_BASIS` (`allocationParcelIds` on a basis other than `PARCEL_SUBSET`).

**The basis** — `COST_ENTRY_BASIS_CONFLICTS_WITH_SPATIAL_LINK` (a basis that spreads across land of its own, also linking a place; the basis is in `params.basis`); `COST_ENTRY_PARCEL_SUBSET_NEEDS_TWO` (a `PARCEL_SUBSET` naming fewer than two distinct parcels — one parcel is a `parcelId` link, not a subset).

**The references** — `REFERENCE_NOT_IN_TENANT` covers every one of them, with which reference in `params.reference`: the six single links (`planting`, `season`, `location`, `parcel`, `lease`, `item`) and, as `parcels`, the `PARCEL_SUBSET` set. **The date** — `COST_ENTRY_INVALID_DATE`, with the field named in `params.field`.

**The currency** — `COST_ENTRY_CURRENCY_NOT_EUR`, with the submitted code in `params.currency`. 201.description: Every created entry, in the order the lines were sent. On a replay, the originally created rows.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

patch.description:
Refusal code: `COST_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND` (404).

Eleven more refusals carry codes, and all of them are 400s.

**The link** — `COST_ENTRY_MULTIPLE_DOMAIN_LINKS` (more than one of the domain links set, count in `params.chosen`); `COST_ENTRY_LEASE_REQUIRES_RENT` (`leaseId` on a non-RENT category); `COST_ENTRY_PARCELS_REQUIRE_SUBSET_BASIS` (`allocationParcelIds` on a basis other than `PARCEL_SUBSET`).

**The basis** — `COST_ENTRY_BASIS_CONFLICTS_WITH_SPATIAL_LINK` (a basis that spreads across land of its own, also linking a place; the basis is in `params.basis`); `COST_ENTRY_PARCEL_SUBSET_NEEDS_TWO` (a `PARCEL_SUBSET` naming fewer than two distinct parcels — one parcel is a `parcelId` link, not a subset).

**The references** — `REFERENCE_NOT_IN_TENANT` covers every one of them, with which reference in `params.reference`: the six single links (`planting`, `season`, `location`, `parcel`, `lease`, `item`) and, as `parcels`, the `PARCEL_SUBSET` set. It is ONE code across the whole API rather than one per surface, so a client handles this refusal once. It answers **400 rather than 404 deliberately**: a 404 would confirm the row exists in SOME tenant, which is what a cross-tenant probe is for. The reference TYPE is returned; the id is not.

**The invoice** — `COST_ENTRY_INVOICE_FILE_NOT_FOUND`, `COST_ENTRY_INVOICE_UPLOAD_INCOMPLETE` (the upload never finished) and `COST_ENTRY_INVOICE_FILE_DELETED`.

**The date** — `COST_ENTRY_INVALID_DATE`, with the field named in `params.field`.

**The currency** — `COST_ENTRY_CURRENCY_NOT_EUR`, with the submitted code in `params.currency`. Costs are recorded in euro: every euro spelling the old free-text field produced is accepted (`EUR`, `EURO`, `EUROS`, `€`, `E`), and anything else is refused. Lev is refused too, which is the non-obvious part — the cost calculator CONVERTS lev at the fixed 1.95583 peg when totalling, so a lev row reads correctly on the calculator while being unsavable here. Those are deliberately different questions: “can this be totalled in euro” and “may this be stored”.

**Changing a legacy row’s currency is refused** — `COST_ENTRY_LEGACY_CURRENCY_LOCKED`, with the stored code in `params.stored`. A row recorded before costs became euro-only keeps its own currency: it is neither converted nor relabelled. Refusing a change TO euro is the point rather than an oversight — rewriting `BGN` to `EUR` without touching `amount` would overstate the cost by the 1.95583 peg, silently. Delete and re-enter the row in euro instead. Omitting `currency` is the no-op, and is what the form does, so editing such a row’s description or supplier needs no special handling. Restating the row’s OWN code verbatim is also accepted, because an unchanged value is not a change.

post.summary: Blend source lots into one output lot
post.description:
Merges several lots into a new one, recording a MERGE edge per source pair so the blend stays traceable in both directions — `/inventory/lots/{id}/trace` walks those edges. 

A lot may NOT appear twice in one blend (the edge is per-pair), every quantity must be positive, and at least one source is required. Each is a 400 with its own message. 

`attributes` is the blended quality result — a weighted combination of the sources, or the overrides supplied.

201.description: The output lot and what went into it.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

patch.description:
Partial update. The whole form is submitted on every edit, so re-sending the current status is a legal no-op that writes nothing.

Refusal code: `CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND` (404).

200.description: The deliveries and the resulting fulfilment.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

THREE PERMISSION codes are described here, and they are the most diffuse of all of them — 106, 51 and 1 call sites respectively, under most mutating and administrative operations in this document:

- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not modify records. Params: `role`. It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

post.description: Appends to the contract’s delivery ledger. Over-delivery is ACCEPTED — the tickets say what they say — and shows up as a complete fulfilment with a `remainingTonnes` floored at zero rather than a negative.

201.description: The created delivery.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

post.summary: Attach an invoice to a cost entry
post.description:
MULTIPART. Uploads the file, mints the FileRecord through the shared storage pipeline, and points the entry at it. There is no generic upload endpoint in this repo — every multipart route mints its own FileRecord as part of an entity write. 

To attach an ALREADY-stored file by id, PATCH the cost entry instead; it runs the same tenant + STORED + not-deleted gate.

201.description: The cost entry, now carrying its invoice.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

get.summary: «Последни стойности» — what the farm last entered
get.description:
The farm's own last value for each OVERHEAD category, so «Нов разход» opens prefilled rather than empty.

**The farm's own history, never a benchmark.** There is no Agrent-wide table behind this — the owner's decision was explicit. A farm with no history gets an empty `overheads` array, and that is the correct first-run state rather than an error.

**Yearly overheads only** — `PAYROLL`, `CREDIT`, `DEPRECIATION`, `OTHER`. `RENT` is deliberately absent: it is a per-decare crop line in the owner's split, not an overhead, however fixed it is.

**`payrollHeadcount` / `payrollAnnualPerPerson` are `null`, never `0`, when a plain total was entered.** Zero people earning a salary is a different claim from "they typed a total", and a prefill that wrote zeros over that distinction would overwrite real figures with a number nobody typed.

**`incurredOn` is returned so a STALE default is visible.** Last year's salary figure prefilled silently is worse than one shown with its date beside it.

**`?commodity=<any spelling>` returns the per-CROP sheet instead** — the farm's last «Култура» lines for that crop, as `{ commodity, lines: [{ category, amountPerDca, currency, incurredOn, description }] }`. Send no `commodity` and you get the overhead payload above, unchanged. The spelling is normalised, so `Canola` resolves to `rapeseed`, and the canonical value is echoed back so you know what was looked up. A commodity the vocabulary does not cover is a **400** carrying `code: "UNKNOWN_COMMODITY"` and the value you sent in `params.commodity`, not an empty sheet: an empty answer is indistinguishable from "this crop has no history", so a typo would read as a fact about the farm.

**It returns the latest SET, not the latest line.** A sheet is several lines entered together — ПРЗ, торове, seed — so every row sharing the most recent `incurredOn` for that crop comes back, each with its own `description` as the row's name. Prefilling only the newest line would collapse a sheet into one and the farmer would retype the rest without noticing.

**`amountPerDca: null` means the farmer entered a TOTAL, not that the line is empty.** The line is returned rather than dropped, so a client can show the row unfilled instead of implying the farm never recorded that cost.

**Read each line's `currency`; do not assume the form's.** Bulgaria moved to EUR in 2026 and older rows are stored in BGN, so prefilling the NUMBER alone shows a 24 000 лв figure as €24 000 — wrong by the fixed 1.95583, and entirely plausible on screen. Convert, or leave a foreign-currency line out and say so.

Carries a weak ETag; send `If-None-Match` and handle **304**.

schema.description: Any spelling the crop vocabulary resolves — `Canola`, `rapeseed`, «рапица». Send it and the 200 is the per-CROP sheet, component `CropCostDefaults`; omit it and the 200 is the overhead payload below, unchanged. The two shapes are DISJOINT, so branch on which key is present rather than on what you sent. A spelling the vocabulary does not cover is a 400 `UNKNOWN_COMMODITY`, never an empty sheet.

parameters.description: Any spelling the crop vocabulary resolves — `Canola`, `rapeseed`, «рапица». Send it and the 200 is the per-CROP sheet, component `CropCostDefaults`; omit it and the 200 is the overhead payload below, unchanged. The two shapes are DISJOINT, so branch on which key is present rather than on what you sent. A spelling the vocabulary does not cover is a 400 `UNKNOWN_COMMODITY`, never an empty sheet.
parameters.name: commodity

200.description:
TWO disjoint shapes, and `commodity` decides which (#1612). Omit it and the response is `CostDefaults`: the farm's latest overhead figures, in a fixed category order so the form's fields do not reorder between visits, empty when the farm has no overhead history. Send it and the response is `CropCostDefaults`, that crop's own sheet.

BRANCH ON WHICH KEY IS PRESENT — `overheads` or `lines` — never on the `anyOf` order. The members are disjoint on their REQUIRED properties, which is the only reason `anyOf` discriminates at all; neither sets `additionalProperties: false`, so a member that later gains an optional key the other requires would make a positional read pick the wrong one with nothing failing.

These two surfaces are single-select and the route wraps each into the array the repository takes — do not send a comma-separated list here expecting the farm-tasks behaviour.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

patch.description:
Partial update. `description` and `resolution` are ENCRYPTED at rest and sanitised server-side on write, so send plain text and expect plain text back.

**Editing is creator-or-admin** (#2169). A writer who did not create the task is refused with `TASK_EDIT_NOT_PERMITTED` — distinct from the role refusal, so a client can tell "this is not yours" from "your role cannot edit tasks" and say so. The check reads `createdByUserId` off the stored ROW, so a patch cannot name its own author.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted to edit THIS task.

- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the role cannot modify records at all.

The middleware 403s listed on the shared envelope are reachable here too.

delete.description:
**A HARD delete.** The row is removed and its children cascade — comments, links and evidence links go with it. This said "Soft delete — reads filter it out, the row survives", which was wrong: `Task.deletedAt` exists and is indexed, and the repository filters on it, but nothing writes it on this path. Corrected 2026-10-23 (#2187).

**Creator-or-admin** (#2187). A writer who did not create the task is refused with `TASK_DELETE_NOT_PERMITTED`, closing an asymmetry #2169 opened: editing was gated and deleting was not, so the weaker permission guarded the more destructive verb. The check reads `createdByUserId` off the STORED row.

`POST /tasks/bulk/delete` raises the SAME code and is **all-or-nothing**: if any selected task was created by somebody else, nothing is deleted and the error carries `refused` and `selected` counts so a client can say how many. A partial success would leave the farmer reconciling an outcome against their own selection with no way to tell which rows went.

**A treatment's task cannot be deleted here at all** (#2220). Four child models cascade on this delete and `OperationParcel` is one of them — those rows ARE the lines the БАБХ ДНЕВНИК prints, and `TaskLink` is the LOCATION link it joins through. So this route would destroy register lines from a filed regulatory document, permanently, while `DELETE /journal/treatments/{treatmentGroupId}` does the same job reversibly: it flags rather than deletes, leaves DONE lines intact, audits the withdrawal and restores from «Кошче».

The discriminator is `treatmentGroupId`, not `type`: a FIELD_OPERATION planned through `POST /locations/{id}/operations` leaves it null and stays deletable here, which matters because the withdrawal route keys on a group such a task does not have.

200.description: Deleted. `{ ok: true }` — no body of the deleted row.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted to delete THIS task.

- `TASK_DELETE_NOT_PERMITTED` — created by somebody else and this caller is not a farm admin. On the bulk route it carries `refused` / `selected`.
- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the role cannot modify records at all.

post.description: The field action. This is the write an operator makes standing in a field, so it is the one that arrives twice: the offline outbox replays it, and the route has an ALREADY-APPLIED arm precisely because its commonest 400 was a replay whose write had already landed. Send `Idempotency-Key` and treat an already-applied response as success, not as a conflict to surface.

400.description:
The state machine refused the move, or a replayed write no longer applies.

- `TASK_STATUS_UNCHANGED` — the task is ALREADY in that status. The commonest cause is the offline outbox replaying a write that already landed, which is why this is the arm to treat as success rather than surface as a conflict. `params.status` names the status it is already in.
- `ILLEGAL_TRANSITION` — a move the state machine does not allow: a CLOSED → OPEN re-open, CANCELED → IN_PROGRESS, or OPEN → CLOSED skipping RESOLVED. `params.from` and `params.to` name both ends, so a client can say which move was refused without guessing.
- `UNKNOWN_TASK_STATUS` — one end of the move is not a status this server knows: a stored value it cannot parse, or a target a newer client sent.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. get.summary: The parcels a task touches, for a map

post.summary: Record the weeds met while doing a task
post.description:
Built for agrent-ios#226 — the weeds half of the task-closing form, filled in by the person standing in the field.

**This is the route a MECHANISATOR can use.** The sibling `POST /agro/parcels/{parcelId}/weed-observations` writes the same row but requires general write permission, which a mechanisator does not have — so closing their own task used to return 403 on the only write the form makes. Here the authorization is **general task write OR being the task's assignee**, and the task id in the path is what bounds the widening. Use this route from a task; use the parcel route for an observation that is not tied to one.

**`parcelId` must be one of the task's own parcels**, resolved by exactly the function behind `GET /tasks/{taskId}/parcels`. So the parcels you can draw on the map are exactly the parcels you can post against, and the two cannot drift. Anything else is `PARCEL_NOT_ON_TASK`, a **400** rather than a 403: the request is mis-addressed, which is a client bug worth surfacing, not a permission the farmer could be granted. That check applies to PRIVILEGED callers too — an editor does not get to post to a parcel the task does not touch.

**One list of weeds, mixed.** The server decides which entries are catalogue keys and which are free text; a client cannot choose the column, which is what keeps the reportable half reportable. An empty resolution is `WEEDS_REQUIRED`.

**Honours `Idempotency-Key`.** Send one, minted BEFORE the first attempt and reused on every retry of the same logical write. The server stores it as `clientMutationId` under a unique `(tenantId, clientMutationId)` index, and a replay returns the ORIGINAL observation with no second audit entry. A replay is **201**, the same as the first write: the response describes the observation that exists, not which attempt filed it, so there is no extra branch to decode.

The read-back is scoped to the PARCEL as well as the tenant, so reusing one key across two parcels is an error rather than a silent mis-delivery — mint a fresh key per logical write. Handing back the row filed against a different parcel would let a client mark its outbox item delivered having lost an observation, and these feed the ДНЕВНИК record: a dropped one misstates what was seen in a field on a date.

The replay read runs AFTER both authorisation gates, so a key alone never returns a row to a caller who could not have written one.

Refusal codes: `TASK_NOT_FOUND` (404, and decided before any permission verdict so a typo'd id never reads as a permission problem), `PARCEL_NOT_ON_TASK` (400), `PARCEL_NOT_FOUND` (404), `WEEDS_REQUIRED` (400).

201.description: The observation exists. Only its `id` is returned — read the parcel's history for the row.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

get.description:

tenants cannot pick between them here. `role` and `tenant` are BOTH `null` when there is no active membership, and they always agree: `role` is never a fallback value, so it is also not proof of access on its own. post.summary: Record that the signed-in user accepts the current terms
post.description:
The way OUT of the consent gate (P3.1). A signed-in session whose `acceptedTermsAt` is null is held at `/accept-terms` by middleware, and every tenant- and person-scoped surface answers `403 Terms acceptance required` until this succeeds.

It exists because the two ways into the product do not agree: `POST /api/auth/register/start` captures acceptance inline, while a first-time Google sign-in creates its user row inside NextAuth and records nothing. Stamping consent on that callback would file an agreement nobody gave, so the product asks instead.

`acceptedTerms` must be literally `true` — checked for identity, not truthiness, so a client that renders no consent control cannot satisfy it with any non-empty value. `termsVersion` must equal the version the server is serving; a mismatch is `400 terms_version_stale` carrying `currentVersion`, which exists so a client can say "reload and read the new terms" rather than showing a generic failure. Render `/terms` to read the current version.

IDEMPOTENT, and it does not re-stamp: a replay by a user who already accepted returns 200 and leaves the stored timestamp alone. That timestamp is the artifact the column exists for, so moving it on every replay would destroy the only thing it is good for.

The session must be refreshed before navigating: `termsPending` is a JWT claim, so a client that writes and redirects without re-minting bounces straight back to the gate.

400.description: `terms_not_accepted` or `terms_version_stale` — a BARE body, not the envelope. The latter carries `currentVersion`, DECLARED here rather than only described, so a generated client has a field to read it from.

401.description: `unauthenticated` — a BARE body, not the envelope.

404.description:

get.summary: A user's uploaded avatar, as webp bytes
get.description:
BINARY, not JSON — `image/webp`, `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` with an `ETag`. This is where a ROOT-RELATIVE `avatarUrl` from `getCurrentUser` points; an ABSOLUTE `avatarUrl` is a third-party provider photo and this route knows nothing about it (see the `avatarUrl` description — the two shapes are fetched differently).

Live since the avatar roadmap P3 and UNDESCRIBED until #1299, so clients were reading its shape out of route code.

ANY authenticated user may fetch ANY user id, deliberately: avatars are rendered across tenant member lists and people-pickers, so a per-viewer check here would break the surfaces the route exists for. Nothing else is exposed — the response is image bytes, and a non-existent user id is indistinguishable from a user with no avatar. Answers a BEARER token as well as a cookie.

The 404 is the ORDINARY case, not an error to log: it is what a user with no uploaded avatar returns, and `<InitialsAvatar>` falls back to initials on it. The bytes are written only through `POST /api/account/avatar`, which accepts the caller's OWN avatar only, validates the webp magic number and AV-scans before the write — so what streams here has passed that gate.

Refusal code: `AVATAR_NOT_FOUND` (404) — no avatar is stored for that user. A user id that does not exist answers the same way, deliberately (see above).

schema.description: The user whose avatar to serve. Any user id, not just the caller — see above.

parameters.description: The user whose avatar to serve. Any user id, not just the caller — see above.
parameters.name: userId

200.description:
The stored avatar. `Content-Type: image/webp`; `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` with an `ETag`, so a changed avatar appears on the NEXT request rather than after a TTL (#1953 — it was `max-age=300`, five minutes of a farmer seeing the picture they just replaced).

`no-cache` is not `no-store`: send `If-None-Match` and a match is answered **304 with no body**, so revalidating costs a few hundred bytes rather than the 5–25 KB of the image. The validator is derived from the stored object’s size and modification time — the same basis a static file server uses — not from a content hash, so two DIFFERENT avatars of identical length written in the same millisecond would share one. The consequence of that collision is a stale picture, never a wrong one.

get.summary: Account — export everything we hold about you
get.description:
A GDPR Art 15 / Art 20 export of the caller’s own personal data, as JSON with `Content-Disposition: attachment`. Machine-readable is what Art 20 asks for and JSON is that; there is no generated archive, because a streamed zip would add a build step and a temp file for no gain at this volume.

**The subject is always the caller.** There is no query parameter and no body: a route that could name a different person would be an arbitrary personal-data read behind somebody’s own session.

**What it includes** is derived from one registry that the erasure also reads (`@/lib/privacy/personal-data-registry`), because a column exported but not erased is a promise broken one way, and a column erased but not exported is data destroyed without ever being shown. A guard derives that registry’s population from the Prisma DMMF, so a new table carrying a person id cannot slip past unclassified.

**What it does NOT include is listed in the response itself**, under `notIncluded`, because Art 15 is a right to know what is held and an export that silently omitted categories would be a worse answer than one that names them. Three omissions are deliberate: FARM RECORDS the caller authored (a journal entry belongs to the farm, which has its own БАБХ retention duty); CREDENTIALS and sessions (a live refresh token in a downloadable file is a risk to the person and answers nothing they asked); and BLOCKS MADE AGAINST THEM, since a social block is silent in both directions by design.

Statements of reasons ARE included, which is a deliberate change of posture from P5.1: that phase gave a recipient no READ POLICY, because a row-level arm would expose `actionId` and through it another party’s moderation rationale. An export is not a policy arm — it runs privileged, for one named person, over their own rows, and the text was emailed to them already. `actionId` is omitted.

Each collection is bounded at 1000 rows and says `truncated` when it hit that, rather than silently returning a prefix. Rate-limited hourly: exercising a data-subject right in bulk is not a thing anyone needs to do.

post.summary: Account — ask for your account to be deleted

Starts a 30-day grace period and FREEZES the account: every live session is revoked immediately. Owner ruling — frozen rather than visible, because a person who asked to be deleted should stop appearing to other farms at once rather than keep showing up in live negotiations for a month. The 30 days protects THEM, from an impulse or a compromised account.

Idempotent, and asking twice does NOT restart the clock — otherwise a person could never actually be deleted. `erasesAt` is returned so a client can state the date rather than recompute it: two places deriving one deadline is two places to get it wrong.

**What happens at the end is pseudonymisation, not deletion, and erasure is INCOMPLETE by design.** The basis is GDPR Art 17(3)(b), legal obligation: the DSA audit trail survives, so a notice this person filed stays linkable to them and the `User` row is kept but emptied — the email becomes a tombstone at an unroutable domain and the name is removed, which also frees the original address for re-registration. Credentials, sessions, social blocks and cohort memberships are DELETED; listings, conversations, messages and enquiries survive with the authorship column overwritten by a random pseudonym, because those rows are also a farm’s or a counterparty’s record. The hash-chained audit logs are untouched: rewriting a row inside one breaks verification for every entry after it.

404 `ACCOUNT_ALREADY_ERASED` when there is nothing left to request.

post.description:
MULTIPART, one part named `file`. Undocumented until #1861, which is how the three `UPLOAD_*` scan codes ended up on `UNDOCUMENTED_BASELINE` with no operation to name them on — the spec described this endpoint’s EFFECTS, in `getUserAvatar`’s description, without describing the endpoint.

The caller’s OWN avatar only; there is no parameter for whose it is. `getUserCtx` refuses an `iflk_` API key presented as a person credential, an MFA-pending session, and the operator-only persona (#1579).

**JPEG or WebP, 4 MB in, re-encoded to a 256×256 WebP of at most 512 KB out (#1903).** Checked on the MAGIC NUMBER, never on a declared content type a caller controls.

This was WebP-only until #1903, which refused every photo an iPhone takes: iOS ImageIO decodes WebP but has no encoder for it (`CGImageDestinationCopyTypeIdentifiers()` does not list `org.webmproject.webp`), so no amount of client work could produce an acceptable file. The server now decodes, applies the EXIF orientation and DROPS it, squares to 256×256 and re-encodes — so EXIF, XMP and GPS are gone for every client rather than only for the web canvas path, which is the privacy guarantee this endpoint exists to make.

The re-encode runs on an already-valid WebP too. A WebP from an unknown client can still carry EXIF, and the point of moving this server-side is that the guarantee should not rest on who the caller is.

**HEIC is deliberately NOT accepted** (owner ruling 2026-10-16). Accepting it would hand attacker-controlled HEIF containers to libheif, and the AV scan ahead of the decode catches known malware signatures rather than a malformed-container parser exploit. The phone converts HEIC to JPEG on device, which iOS can do. PNG is likewise absent: the web canvas already converts one to WebP before upload.

AV-scanned before the write AND before the decode, so the scanner reads the bytes the caller actually sent — a signature describes that artefact, not a re-encode nobody uploaded. The size is checked twice on purpose: once on `file.size` before buffering, so an oversized upload never reaches memory, and once on the buffer.

**Refusal codes.**
- `AVATAR_FILE_MISSING` — no `file` part in the form data.
- `AVATAR_EMPTY` — the part was present and zero bytes.
- `AVATAR_TOO_LARGE` — the upload is over 4 MB, or the re-encoded result somehow exceeded 512 KB. Raised at either size check.
- `AVATAR_FORMAT_NOT_ALLOWED` — the magic number is neither JPEG nor WebP. Convert and retry; do not retry the same bytes. Replaces `AVATAR_NOT_WEBP`, which named the one format the endpoint no longer requires.
- `AVATAR_UNREADABLE` — the magic number said JPEG or WebP and the decoder disagreed, so the container is truncated or malformed. A different photo, not the same one re-exported.
- `UPLOAD_INFECTED` — the malware scanner identified something. Refused in every scan mode.
- `UPLOAD_SCANNER_UNAVAILABLE` — a scanner IS configured, it errored, and the deployment asked to fail closed. Transient; retrying later is reasonable.

`UPLOAD_UNSCANNED_ON_PUBLIC_SURFACE` is NOT reachable here: this surface declares `exposure: private`, and that code fires only for a public one. No caller in the product passes `public` today.

- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.

Each carries a `message`. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. - `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.

put.summary: Submit a reviewer verdict for one subject
put.description:
A discriminated union on `decision`: `CONFIRM`, `REVOKE`, or `MODIFY` with a target role. The first submission on a campaign moves it `OPEN` → `IN_REVIEW` — see `transitionedToInReview`.

**A REVOKE is recorded here and APPLIED at close.** Submitting one does not remove anybody; `POST /close` executes them. So a client must not report access as withdrawn on a 200 from this operation.

**Refusal codes.**
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_NOT_FOUND` — no such campaign in this farm.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISION_NOT_FOUND` — the campaign exists but holds no such decision row. Usually a stale client: the roster is snapshotted, so a decision id from a different campaign will not resolve here.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_NOT_ASSIGNED_REVIEWER` — the caller is not the campaign’s assigned reviewer. A permission shortfall that no role lifts, because the constraint is identity rather than tier: an OWNER who is not the reviewer is refused too, which is the point of assigning one.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISION_ALREADY_RECORDED` — a verdict is already on this row. Decisions are recorded once, so changing one is two steps: `POST .../revoke` to clear it, then submit again.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISIONS_IMMUTABLE` — the campaign is closed, so its decisions are frozen. Retrying cannot work and no role lifts it.

post.summary: Clear a recorded verdict so it can be decided again
post.description:
Returns the decision row to undecided. **Nothing is deleted** — the row stays on the campaign and still needs a verdict, which is why this is a `POST` to a sub-resource rather than a `DELETE` on the decision: a client treating it as a deletion would stop showing a subject who is still awaiting review.

`reason` is REQUIRED (3–2000 chars) and is written into the `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISION_REVOKED` audit entry alongside the verdict being cleared. Reversing a decision on an audited control is itself an auditable act, so there is no way to do it without saying why.

After this, `PUT .../decisions/{decisionId}` accepts a new verdict — the pair is how a verdict gets changed, since submission is once-only.

**Refusal codes.**
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISION_NOT_FOUND` — no such decision row on this campaign. Also returned when the row is concurrently executed between the gate and the write, so a client should re-read rather than retry blindly.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_NOT_FOUND` — no such campaign in this farm.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_NOT_ASSIGNED_REVIEWER` — identity, not tier: an OWNER who is not the assigned reviewer is refused, exactly as on submit.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISIONS_IMMUTABLE` — the campaign is closed. Nothing lifts this; a closed campaign is the audit record.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISION_NOT_RECORDED` — the row holds no verdict, so there is nothing to clear. Distinguished from a missing row so a client can tell "already undecided" from "wrong id".
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISION_ALREADY_EXECUTED` — the verdict has been applied against the live membership and cannot be taken back here. Undoing an executed revocation means re-granting access, which is a membership operation and not a review one.

post.summary: Close a campaign and execute its revocations
post.description:
The only operation that CHANGES anyone’s access. Every `REVOKE` recorded during the campaign is applied here, a PDF artifact is generated as evidence of the close, and the campaign becomes `CLOSED` and immutable.

`evidenceFileRecordId` may be `null` — the artifact is evidence OF the close rather than a precondition for it, so a storage failure does not block closing.

**Refusal codes.**
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_NOT_FOUND` — no such campaign in this farm.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_ALREADY_CLOSED` — it is closed. Idempotent in effect but reported rather than silently accepted, because a second close would generate a second evidence artifact for one event.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_DECISIONS_PENDING` — subjects remain undecided. A campaign closed with gaps would be an audit record asserting a review that did not happen, so the refusal is the control: decide the rest, then close.
- `ACCESS_REVIEW_WOULD_ORPHAN_OWNERS` — executing the revocations would leave the farm with no OWNER. Refused regardless of role, including for an OWNER revoking themselves: a farm nobody can administer cannot be recovered through the product.

Streams the artifact generated at close. `Content-Disposition` carries the stored filename, which may be Cyrillic.

**Refusal codes.** These are the shared evidence-file codes rather than campaign ones, because the refusals are about the FILE:
- `EVIDENCE_FILE_NOT_FOUND` — the campaign names an artifact that no longer resolves.

Two 404s on this path are still UNCODED — a missing campaign, and a campaign that has never generated an artifact. They are #1712 work rather than this registration’s, and a client should treat an uncoded 404 here as "no artifact available".

get.summary: Vegetation and moisture risk for one parcel
get.description:
Sentinel-2-derived NDVI/NDMI means and traffic-light levels. Cached server-side per (tenant, parcel, day) for 6h and served with a weak ETag — send `If-None-Match` and expect 304, because the first call of the day is a live Earth Engine query and the rest are free.

The parcel id is a PATH segment, deliberately. iOS writes the full request URL — query included — to the unified log from its own networking layer, below anything an app can suppress.

get.summary: Parcels this tenant has already asked about
get.description:
Ids only, ETagged. **Informational — do NOT use it to disable the ask.**
