post.summary: Ask an insurer for an offer on a parcel
post.description:
**Irreversible, and now repeatable.** There is still no DELETE and no withdraw — a lead persists once written. What changed on 2026-09-24 is that the unique on (parcel, tenant) was dropped, so a parcel may carry SEVERAL leads: the form collects the farmer's own land size, and a figure they got wrong the first time could not otherwise be corrected.

Consequences for a client:
- A second POST no longer returns 409. It creates another lead and emails the operator again.
- **Do not disable the control** because `GET /insurance/leads` lists the parcel. That endpoint is now INFORMATIONAL — suppressing the trigger makes the re-ask this change exists to allow unreachable.
- Still do not fire it against a real parcel to test wiring: every lead is an email to the platform operator, who has to reconcile duplicates by hand.

Lead-gen only: the row is stored, a confirmation notification is written for the REQUESTER and a copy is sent to the operator. No insurer API is called and no other tenant is contacted, which is what separates this from an exchange inquiry. Opened by the three-step calculator on Farm risk, which previews the premium and posts only the four quote INPUTS. Rate-limited on its OWN tier (INSURANCE_LEAD_LIMIT, 20 per hour): every lead emails the operator, and the inquiry tier's per-minute window allowed 600 of those an hour.

201.description:
The lead was recorded. **Honours `Idempotency-Key`** — replaying a request with the same key returns the ORIGINAL lead, with no second row, no second audit entry and no second operator email. The key is scoped to the requesting tenant and must be 1-128 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`.

When the body carried a `quote`, the response echoes the figures the SERVER computed. A premium sent by the client is ignored: the request schema has no price field and strips one if present.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

THREE PERMISSION codes are described here, and they are the most diffuse of all of them — 106, 51 and 1 call sites respectively, under most mutating and administrative operations in this document:

- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not modify records. Params: `role`. It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

get.summary: The insurance product catalogue and its tariffs
get.description:
For clients that cannot import the pricing engine. The web app does not need this — it imports the same constant the engine uses — so it exists for a SEPARATE codebase, where a compiled-in tariff is a second description of one thing.

That duplication is worse than most, because it is asymmetric: the SERVER recompute is what gets stored and emailed, so a stale local tariff shows the farmer one figure and the operator another, with nothing on either side saying so. Fetch this rather than hardcoding `tariffBp`.

`engineVersion` is the rounding rules the tariffs belong to. Do not send it anywhere — compare it, so a preview built against version N notices the server has moved to N+1.

Language is DECLARED, not negotiated: pass `?locale=bg` (or rely on the `NEXT_LOCALE` cookie). `Accept-Language` is deliberately ignored — a device set to English-language/Bulgarian-region would otherwise pull English product names onto an entirely Bulgarian screen. Absent both, the answer is English, so a client that wants Bulgarian must say so.

The labels here are the SOURCE for native clients; where five of them overlap a client's own commodity names, that equality is intentional — change `insurance.products.<key>.name` in `messages/` and both follow.

schema.description: Which language to resolve `name` and `blurb` in. DECLARE it — `Accept-Language` is deliberately ignored, and the fallback is the `NEXT_LOCALE` cookie then `en`. A client whose UI is Bulgarian by declaration rather than by device setting must send `bg` on every request; a device reporting English-language/Bulgarian-region would otherwise be served English names for an entirely Bulgarian screen.

get.summary: What a parcel has grown, and what was done to it
get.description:
One request for the whole archive: authored crop seasons, COMPLETED field operations, and weed observations, each newest-first.

`parcel.cropType` is the CURRENT crop and is a single overwritten field — it carries no year and no history, which is the reason `cropSeasons` exists. Do not infer this year from it and the rest from the archive; the archive is the record.

ETagged: a parcel grows one crop a season but the screen is revisited often. The tag is derived from the BODY, so each page validates separately and a cached first page is never served for a second.

**Three lists, three cursors.** The sections have three different sort keys — harvest YEAR, completion date, observation date — so there is no single position to page from. Each list carries its own `…Cursor`, null when that list has no older rows, and you page each independently: a parcel with 200 operations and 3 crop seasons returns a cursor for the operations only.

**Each list defaults to 100 rows** and `limit` applies PER LIST, so a client knows whether a first page can even be partial before it decides to offer a "load older" control at all.

**A stale or malformed cursor RESTARTS that list — and it does so with a 200.** That is deliberate server-side: a 400 over yesterday's cursor would strand a screen for no gain. But it means the failure arrives as a VALID BODY holding the NEWEST rows, so a client that appends a page blindly gets an infinite list with nothing erroring — page one arrives, its cursor goes back, page one arrives — and a farmer sees one spray recorded forty times and concludes the app is lying about his own field. Deduplicate each append by `id`, and treat a page that adds nothing new as the end of that list. The same rule covers a genuinely empty page, which is why a client does not need to tell the two apart.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. - `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. post.description:
Back-fillable on purpose — years long before the farm started using this system are accepted, because an archive whose earliest entry is today is not an archive.

`cropType` is NOT validated against the crop catalogue. Live data already holds values outside it, and refusing them would make the farm's own history un-recordable. Offer the catalogue in the picker; accept what they grew.

A parcel may hold more than one season in a year — a catch crop after an early harvest is ordinary practice, so this is not refused as a duplicate.

get.summary: Every task that touches this parcel
get.description:
What «Блокове» → a parcel shows beneath its risk: the parcel's whole task history, newest first, in the same row shape as `/tasks`.

**Use this rather than `GET /tasks?linkedEntityType=PARCEL`.** That filter returns the scouting and hand-made tasks and silently OMITS every planned spray and fertilising, because a field operation reaches its parcels through its operation lines rather than through a `PARCEL` task link. The answer looks complete and is missing most of what was done to the field. This operation unions both sources and deduplicates by task id.

**Every status is returned, terminal ones included.** The current/archive split is the client's: `RESOLVED` / `CLOSED` / `CANCELED` are archive, the rest are current. That grouping is deliberately NOT server-side — the status enum is already the contract, so a server-side split would freeze a UI decision behind a deploy.

**`truncated` means the list is a PREFIX of the history**, from either of two caps: the rendered page, or the upstream id read on a parcel with an extreme number of jobs. Read it — a cut history that does not say so is indistinguishable from a complete one.

Ordered `createdAt` descending, with `id` as a tie-break so the order is TOTAL: a treatment writes several tasks in the same millisecond, and an unstable order would make the truncation boundary move between requests.

There is no `limit` or cursor, deliberately: one shape, so a client needs one branch. The parcel id is a path segment rather than a query parameter because iOS writes the full URL including the query to the device log.

NOT cached server-side, unlike `/tasks` — a farmer opens this right after recording work on the field, and the id union depends on `OperationParcel`, which writes no `Task` row and so would not invalidate a task-keyed cache.

200.description: The parcel's tasks, newest first. `mayDelete` is per-caller and always computed here — read `mayDelete === false`, never `!mayDelete`.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

Signed in, but not permitted.

- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. - `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. get.summary: A parcel’s comments and closing notes
get.description:
The history under «Блокове» → a parcel: every task comment and every closing note on the tasks that touched this parcel, newest first, in ONE read.

Over the same task set as `listParcelTasks` — both resolve it the same way — so the history and the task list on one screen cannot disagree about which tasks touched the parcel.

**Two kinds in one list.** `COMMENT` is a task comment; `RESOLUTION` is the note left when the task was closed. They are merged server-side because the screen is one chronological history, and a client assembling it from two lists would have to re-derive an ordering the server already knows.

`createdAt` is ONE field for both kinds — the comment’s own time, or the task’s close time for a resolution — so a client sorts and renders a single key.

`createdBy` is **null on a RESOLUTION**, and that is a statement about the data rather than a gap: `Task.resolution` is a column with no author, so naming the assignee or the last status-changer would attribute the note to somebody the row does not identify.

`truncated` has the same two causes as `listParcelTasks`: this page’s cap, or the upstream task-id read on a parcel with an extreme number of jobs. Either means the history is a PREFIX — do not infer completeness from the row count.

No query string, deliberately — the parcel id is a path segment because iOS writes the full URL including the query to the device log.

It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. get.summary: An AI briefing over the farm's fields
get.description:
Generated from satellite index means plus the farm's own records. Cached, so two calls in a day return the same `generatedAt`.

post.summary: Борса — open the conversation for a listing
post.description:
**Idempotent.** A second call returns the thread that already exists rather than creating another, so a client may call it on every "message seller" tap without checking first. **201** means one was created, **200** that one was already open — both carry the same body.

Messages come back OLDEST-FIRST (reading order), but are selected newest-first and reversed — so a long thread returns its END, not its beginning.

Scroll back with `before`: pass the response's `olderCursor` to fetch the page immediately older than the one you hold. `olderCursor: null` means you have reached the start of the conversation.

`unreadCount` is counted in the DATABASE, not over the returned page, so it is a true count rather than one capped at `limit`.

The replay check runs BEFORE the party, block and closed checks, so a retry of a message that was already accepted returns its original result even if the seller has since blocked the sender. Otherwise a flaky link turns "delivered" into a 403 for a message that IS in the thread. Without a key the send is NOT idempotent — two taps make two messages. **Two different block refusals, and the difference is deliberate (P5.2b).** 403 `THREAD_BLOCKED` is the EXCHANGE block — a seller farm refusing a buyer — and it says so in words, because a commercial refusal is something a buyer is entitled to understand. 403 `THREAD_PERSON_BLOCKED` is the PERSON block and can only ever reach the BLOCKER: "you have blocked this person". A client that retries on its own schedule spends the next window the moment it opens and stays blocked; the header says when the budget is actually free. A blocked sender consumes quota too — the limit runs before the block check, so the cost of being blocked falls on the blocked party. **Either party may close, and closing does not lock the thread.** Sending a message reopens it, which is why there is no reopen endpoint to pair with this one — the way back is the thing you were going to do anyway.

get.description:

get.description:
The GLOBAL aggregated news feed, newest first, optionally filtered by `category`, by `tags` (comma-separated, ANY-OF) and by a `q` search over title and summary, paged by an opaque `cursor`. Tenant-agnostic payload; the tenant in the path authenticates the caller. 

**`tags` ignores keys it does not recognise rather than returning 400.** A client passes its stored preferences straight into this parameter, so a tag the server has since renamed would otherwise turn a saved preference into a broken feed. If every key is unrecognised the feed is UNFILTERED, not empty — read the `tags` echo in the response to tell that apart from a full feed. (`PUT /api/me/news-preferences` is deliberately the opposite and 400s on an unknown tag: there a person is choosing, and a typo is a client bug worth surfacing.) 

**Preferences are not applied implicitly.** The payload is cached under a key shared by every reader, so filtering by the caller’s own preferences would write one person’s feed into the entry everybody else reads. Resolve your preferences client-side and pass `tags`. 

`q` searches at most the last 60 days — `RETENTION_DAYS` deletes older rows on every pull — so finding nothing from last spring is correct behaviour, and an empty state should say so rather than read as a failure. Note that `q` travels in the query string, which iOS logs in full and unsuppressably; a crop name is low-sensitivity, but do not put anything stronger there. 

Carries a weak ETag; send `If-None-Match` and handle **304**. Cached 1h server-side, except a `q` search, which is a live read every time (the key space of a free-text query is unbounded and would evict the shared feed) — the ETag still answers 304 for a repeated identical search.

get.description:
Every tag `NewsItem.tags` can contain, grouped, with Bulgarian and English labels. Build a tag filter or a preferences sheet from THIS rather than from a hard-coded list: the vocabulary is the server's, and a tag added here appears in the client with no app release.

**Exactly two groups, `crops` then `topics`, and that is contract.** Do not flatten them — the grouping is what a sectioned picker renders from, and a client decoding a flat array breaks the moment a third group is added.

**Treat an unrecognised tag key as a tag you cannot label, not as an error.** This list grows. An article may legitimately carry a key your build has never seen; show it using the `label` from this response rather than dropping the article.

**Tenant-agnostic.** The vocabulary is identical for every farm; the tenant in the path authenticates the caller. `Cache-Control: private, max-age=86400` — hold it for a day. It also carries a weak ETag, so `If-None-Match` gets a **304** if you revalidate sooner.

get.summary: «Цени» — what is typed, and what the feed says
get.description:
One row for EVERY commodity a superuser may override, not only those with an override: the form is a list of fields rather than a list of existing entries, so a commodity with neither a typed nor a feed price is a row with both null, which is a true statement about it.

Each row carries `entryUnit`, the denomination the POST will store the value under. Read it rather than holding a copy: the nine crops and fertilisers are `EUR/t` and diesel alone is `EUR/l`, and a client with its own copy of that split is a second source of truth whose disagreement is not an error but a price wrong by a factor of a thousand.

`apiFeed: "none"` and `api: null` are different claims and both matter — see the field descriptions. Three of the ten commodities have no free feed anywhere, so for those a typed price is not an override at all, it is the only source.

post.summary: Type a day of prices that win for every farm
post.description:
Owner ruling 2026-10-10: a typed price **always wins** over the API, on every surface and for every farm, until a superuser CLEARS it. A manual override, not a stale-only fallback — chosen over "API unless missing or stale" and over "newest wins".

**One DAY, all or nothing.** Up to ten commodities in one transaction, so a refusal on the tenth rolls back the first nine. A day that half-commits is worse than one that failed, because the superuser cannot tell which prices are live — and these move every farm’s calculator.

**Unit and currency are NOT accepted from you.** They are derived server-side per commodity, and that is deliberate: a caller that could choose the unit could put a per-tonne figure into the litre series, and the six-column natural key `(source, commodity, region, stage, currency, unit)` would dutifully create it. `entryUnit` on the GET tells you what will be used, as a label and a sanity check — never as an input.

**The override is published as its own series** with a fixed `source: "platform"`, region `BG`, in the derived unit. It appears in the same market-prices payload Тенденции and Табло already read, beside the feed’s series. For the calculator’s reference price it SUPPRESSES every feed series for that commodity — suppressed, not averaged and not offered as comparable, because consumers group by currency or refuse and never blend.

**A client must prefer a marked override ACROSS unit groups, not within one.** Ranking normally happens inside a `(unit, currency)` group, and the diesel bulletin is published in `EUR/1000l` while a typed diesel price is `EUR/l` — so an override in a different group is never compared against the feed and is never chosen. Marking the series is necessary and not sufficient.

**The 400s this raises, by `error.code`, so a client can switch on them rather than show a generic message:**

- `DUPLICATE_COMMODITY` — the same commodity appears twice in one day, with it named in `params.commodity`. The feeds average genuine duplicate observations; two prices typed for one commodity on one day is a typo, and averaging a typo produces a number nobody entered while taking the last silently discards the first.
- `UNKNOWN_COMMODITY` — a spelling the vocabulary does not resolve, echoed in `params.commodity`.
- `COMMODITY_NOT_OVERRIDABLE` — a commodity the vocabulary KNOWS but the owner has not opened to overrides. A different thing to fix from a typo: `oats` has no feed either and is a plausible thing to try, but widening the list is a decision rather than a retry.
- `OVERRIDE_DENOMINATION_CHANGED` — a live override for that commodity is recorded in a different unit or currency from the one the server now derives, with both in `params` as `stored` and `expected`. Clear it before typing a new one: two live overrides for one commodity in different denominations is an ambiguity no consumer can resolve, so this refuses rather than minting a second series.

Any of them refuses the WHOLE day, before anything is written.

**`clientMutationId` is recorded, not relied on.** Send it in the body or as `Idempotency-Key` — both are honoured, so you need not discover which. But idempotency here comes from the point upsert on `(seriesId, date)`: re-sending a day produces the identical state. These are GLOBAL tables with no `tenantId`, so the `(tenantId, clientMutationId)` convention used by the cost batch is not available and is not needed — a cost sheet accumulates, a price day does not.

Gated on `admin.manage` **inside** `PLATFORM_TENANT_SLUG`. Both halves are load-bearing: `admin.manage` is held by the OWNER of EVERY tenant, so alone it would hand any farm’s owner the global price cache. The gate FAILS CLOSED — unset slug means 404 for everyone, the owner included.

delete.summary: Clear the override, handing authority back to the feed
delete.description:
Ends the override run for one commodity, across every region and stage. The feed becomes authoritative again and the `platform` series is **absent from the payload entirely** — "no platform position" is a different claim from "a platform position of nothing".

**It MARKS; it does not delete.** The series and its points are stamped, so the typed history survives and so does the audit trail of what was typed. The read path excludes a cleared series and its stamped points, which is what makes "cleared" and "absent" the same thing to a client without the rows going anywhere.

**Re-typing after a clear starts a FRESH run.** Points from before the clear are never republished. A clear is an affirmative withdrawal, not a mute: if clearing hid points that reappeared on the next type, a superuser who cleared a wrong price would see it resurrected by an unrelated later entry. This is why the stamp is on the POINT as well as the series — the natural key is unique, so a re-type resolves to the same series row, and un-clearing that row alone would bring the whole previous run back.

**Clearing nothing is a 200 with `cleared: false`**, not a 404. A client retrying a clear is the normal case rather than the odd one.

For a commodity whose `apiFeed` is `"none"`, clearing leaves the calculator with NO price for that crop — a client should say so before confirming, because it will look like data loss otherwise. A request body is ignored.

Same gate as the write, failing closed the same way.

get.description:
The active Борса feed, keyset-paginated. Page size defaults to 50 and is capped at 100; pass `cursor` back VERBATIM from `nextCursor` and stop when it is null. 

`side`, `kind`, `commodity` and `region` are COMMA-SEPARATED multi-value params in ONE parameter (`?side=SELL&kind=CULTURE,SEEDS`) — a multi-select facet arrives joined, and a bad member is a clean 400 rather than a 500. `commodity` is opaque free text, not an enum: a seller types it on the create form. 

`q` also matches Bulgarian oblast NAMES against stored English region names, so «Пловдив» finds a listing whose `regionName` is "Plovdiv". 

Carries a weak ETag; send `If-None-Match` and handle **304**.

schema.description:
Free text, matched against the commodity AND the oblast, in Bulgarian or English. One field; the server decides which axis a term belongs to.

**Prefixes work in both languages.** «пше» and `whea` both find wheat, as «пшеница» and `wheat` do. The two halves get there by different routes, which is worth knowing if a result ever looks asymmetric: the column stores the ENGLISH slug, so an English prefix matches the stored value directly, while a Bulgarian prefix is resolved against the alias vocabulary first and then matched exactly. Before this, «пшеница» worked and «пше» did not.

**Two folded characters minimum** for the prefix resolution. A single letter is a keystroke on the way to a word rather than a query — «с» alone starts both слънчоглед and соя — so one character resolves no commodity. Folding removes case, spaces, dots and hyphens, so `Sun-Flo` is the same query as `sunflo`.

**An ambiguous prefix returns everything it matches**, which is the answer rather than an error: `so` finds both soybean and wheat (via `softwheat`). Do not treat several results as a failed lookup.

**Oblast names match on any substring**, Bulgarian or English, so «Пле» finds Плевен. That axis never had the exact-match floor the commodity axis had.

Inputs the farm BUYS are deliberately unresolvable: «диз» finds nothing, because the exchange does not trade diesel.

post.description:
Publishes a listing for the calling tenant. Requires the EXCHANGE module — 403 `module_disabled: EXCHANGE` otherwise. Rate-limited separately from ordinary writes.

put.description:
Replaces EVERY editable field on a listing the caller owns. Owner ruling 2026-10-31: every field is editable, including side, kind and commodity.

A full replacement rather than a partial patch, and the reason is the nullable fields: under a patch, "leave the description alone" and "clear the description" are the same JSON. The seller's own read carries `edit`, which is this body verbatim.

A later `expiresAt` REACTIVATES an EXPIRED listing (EXPIRED → ACTIVE), keeping its conversations. `null` counts as later, because no expiry is later than any date. The plan's ACTIVE-listing limit is checked only on that transition, since an ordinary edit cannot change the count.

Unlike withdraw, this REQUIRES the EXCHANGE module: that exemption exists because the toggle governs participation in the marketplace rather than custody of rows you already posted, and editing changes what is being offered.

Refusals, each a distinct `code`: LISTING_NOT_FOUND; LISTING_NOT_OWNED when the listing belongs to another tenant; LISTING_TERMINAL for a withdrawn or fulfilled listing, which cannot be edited; LISTING_MODIFIED when `updatedAt` no longer matches, so a concurrent edit is refused rather than silently overwritten; LISTING_REGION_UNKNOWN for an unrecognised `regionCode`. LISTING_EXPIRES_AT_IN_PAST when a CHANGED `expiresAt` is not in the future — an UNCHANGED one is always accepted, whatever the clock says, because `edit` round-trips the date as a string and a client that does not touch it sends it back verbatim. Refusing that would reject an edit to a listing on its last day for a field nobody changed.

Answers with the listing AND its new `edit` object, so a client can render the result and repopulate the form without a second read.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. 404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

409.description:

Those carry `details.currentVersion` / `expectedVersion` off a version counter and are resolved by merging; this precondition is a TIMESTAMP, carries no `details`, and the edit is a full replacement, so the only remedy is to reload the form. A client keying on `STALE_DATA` will not match it, which is intended — the two want different sentences.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

get.description:

200.description: The buyer’s outbox. Empty array when it has sent none.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

post.description:
Sends an inquiry to a listing’s seller. Answers with the id and status ONLY — not the inquiry projection — because the buyer’s contact has not been shared yet and the reveal gate lives in that projection. 

Refusals, each a distinct `code`: LISTING_NOT_FOUND; LISTING_NOT_ACTIVE when the listing has left ACTIVE; LISTING_EXPIRED when its `expiresAt` has passed, which the browse feed already filters on; LISTING_IS_YOUR_OWN when the listing belongs to the calling tenant; and INQUIRY_ALREADY_SENT. The seller is notified; contact details are exchanged only if they ACCEPT.

201.description: The created inquiry’s id and status.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

patch.summary: Борса — accept or decline an inquiry
patch.description:
The SELLER’s decision on an inquiry against their own listing. ACCEPTED completes the two-sided consent and is what populates `counterpartyContact` and `contactSharedAt` on both sides; DECLINED leaves both null permanently. 

Refusals carry a distinct `code`: INQUIRY_NOT_FOUND; INQUIRY_NOT_PENDING when it has already been answered; and INQUIRY_ACCEPT_REQUIRES_ACTIVE_LISTING when ACCEPT is attempted on a listing that has left ACTIVE — accepting would reveal contact details for a deal that can no longer happen, and DECLINE still works, which is the part the sentence has to carry. It was LISTING_NOT_ACTIVE until #2564.

Answers with the id and new status only.

Refusal code: `INQUIRY_NOT_FOUND` (404). ONE oracle for “not yours” and “not there”: a caller who is not the seller gets the same 404 as for a missing inquiry, so an outsider cannot confirm another tenant’s private buyer↔seller conversation by enumerating ids. Do not branch on it as “missing”.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

get.description:
Opened by the app in an `ASWebAuthenticationSession`, NOT fetched. Stashes the PKCE challenge and the app’s delivery URI in a short-lived HttpOnly cookie and hands off to the existing NextAuth provider flow — nothing about provider sign-in is reimplemented. 

`redirect_uri` is checked against an allowlist; an unlisted one is a 400 `redirect_uri_not_allowed` rather than a redirect, which is what stops this being an open redirect. 

The challenge lives in the cookie rather than in the OAuth `state` because `state` round-trips through the provider and lands in browser history.

schema.description: Where the CODE should be delivered. Allowlisted.

parameters.description: Where the CODE should be delivered. Allowlisted.
parameters.name: redirect_uri

schema.description: PKCE challenge (S256).

parameters.description: PKCE challenge (S256).
parameters.name: code_challenge

schema.description: S256. Anything else is a 400.

parameters.description: S256. Anything else is a 400.
parameters.name: code_challenge_method

schema.description: Defaults to google. An unknown one is a 400.

parameters.description: Defaults to google. An unknown one is a 400.
parameters.name: provider

302.description: Redirect to the provider via NextAuth. Follow it in the browser session; there is no body.

400.description: `invalid_request`, `unsupported_code_challenge_method`, `redirect_uri_not_allowed` or `unsupported_provider` — a BARE body, not the `ErrorResponse` envelope. The first two are RFC 6749 §5.2 / RFC 7636 codes; branch on the string.

get.summary: Mint the code and hand it to the app
get.description:
Reached by the SYSTEM browser after the provider flow has set a session cookie. Reads the handoff cookie, mints a short-lived PKCE-bound code against the session that now exists, and redirects to the app’s URI carrying the CODE AND NOTHING ELSE — no token, no identity. 

The code is single-use and short-lived; it is spent at `/exchange`. 

**401 `not_authenticated`** means the browser reached here without a session — the provider step did not complete, and the client must restart at `/start`.

303.description: Redirect to the app’s registered URI with the single-use code. No body.

400.description: `no_handoff`, `invalid_handoff` or `redirect_uri_not_allowed` — a BARE body, not the envelope.

401.description: `not_authenticated` or `session_invalid` — a BARE body, not the envelope.

post.summary: Sign in with Apple — identity token to token pair
post.description:
The one native sign-in that does NOT go through the system browser. `ASAuthorizationController` hands the app an identity token directly, so there is no `/start`, no code and no PKCE verifier: this single call IS the sign-in. Unauthenticated by construction — the identity token is the credential — and rate-limited at the pre-auth tier. 

**The nonce is single-use.** Generate a fresh random `nonce` per attempt, pass its SHA-256 to Apple as the request nonce, and send the RAW value here. The server checks the hash matches the token AND claims the nonce exactly once, so a replayed token is refused even though its signature is still valid. Never reuse a nonce across attempts. 

**Every verification failure is `400 { "error": "invalid_grant" }`** — bad signature, wrong audience, expired token, mismatched nonce and replayed nonce are indistinguishable ON PURPOSE. Do not branch on the reason; start a fresh authorisation. 

Two answers are deliberately distinguishable, because both are actionable and neither describes the token: `503 apple_sign_in_disabled` means the server has no Apple audience configured (an operator task, not a client bug), and `400 email_required` means Apple sent no email on what is a FIRST authorisation — request the email scope. 

**A first sign-in returns `termsPending: true`.** There is no browser here, so nothing showed the terms before the account existed. Present them and call `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` with the bearer; until then every tenant and person route answers 403. That route is reachable while pending, as is this one. 

Apple sends `email` only on the FIRST authorisation — the account is keyed on Apple’s stable `sub`, so later sign-ins need no email and must not be treated as new users.

200.description: The token pair, plus `termsPending` so the client knows whether to present the terms before doing anything else.

202.description: The farm requires a second factor and this request declared it can collect one (a `code_challenge` was sent). No token pair yet — redeem the ticket at `POST /api/auth/native/mfa`.

400.description: `invalid_grant` — a BARE body. Covers a bad signature, the wrong audience, an expired token, a nonce mismatch and a replayed nonce, deliberately indistinguishable.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
The farm requires a second factor this request cannot collect.

`error.code` is `MFA_REQUIRED` whenever **no `code_challenge` was sent**. A client that did not opt in cannot show a code screen and does not know the enrolment code either, so it gets the one code it understands — the same opt-in rule as the 202 above. Use Google or Microsoft, or the web.

It is `MFA_ENROLLMENT_REQUIRED` only for a client that DID send a `code_challenge` and whose account has no verified authenticator. There is no shared secret to check a code against, so the remedy is enrolment on the web rather than another provider — two codes because the two remedies differ, and gated on the opt-in so an older build never receives one it would render as a generic refusal.

post.summary: Redeem a pending-MFA ticket with a TOTP code
post.description:
The second half of Apple sign-in at a farm that requires a second factor. `signInWithApple` returned `202` with a ticket; post it here with the six-digit code and the verifier whose challenge you sent. 

**Only reachable for Apple.** Google and Microsoft sign-in goes through the system browser, so their code is typed in the sign-in sheet and `completeNativeSignIn` simply withholds the auth code until it clears. There is no sheet in the Apple flow, which is why this endpoint exists at all — it is not a general-purpose MFA endpoint and the web does not use it. 

**The ticket is not a credential.** It is opaque, single-use, server-stored hashed, five-minute, and PKCE-bound; it carries no claims and authenticates nothing. `exchangeNativeAuthCode` cannot redeem it — that endpoint looks only for session codes, so a ticket is not found there rather than refused by a check. 

**Five wrong codes burn the ticket.** The cap is on the TICKET, not on an IP or an account, so it bounds exactly one sign-in attempt and cannot be sidestepped by reconnecting. It matches the web challenge's allowance, so the number of tries does not depend on which device somebody is holding. Expect `429` with `Retry-After` if the shared per-user limiter trips first. 

**On success you get the ordinary token pair**, with `termsPending` exactly as `signInWithApple` returns it — a first Apple sign-in can owe both a second factor and the terms.

200.description: The factor was accepted. The ticket is consumed and this is the token pair.

400.description: `error.code` is `MFA_CODE_INVALID` when the ticket is fine and the CODE was wrong — `error.params.attemptsRemaining` is an integer, and at `0` the ticket is already burned by this same response, so say "too many wrong codes, sign in again" without another call to find out. It is `MFA_CODE_MALFORMED` when six digits were not supplied; that costs no attempt, because input that was never a guess should not spend one of five tries.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description: `error.code` is `MFA_TICKET_INVALID`. ONE code for expired, consumed, unknown, wrong-purpose and PKCE-mismatched tickets, deliberately indistinguishable — the remedy is identical in every case (start sign-in again), and telling a caller which of five checks defeated it is free help to somebody probing. Do not branch on it beyond restarting.

get.summary: Turn a native bearer into a webview cookie session
get.description:
NOT part of the sign-in sequence. A Capacitor shell renders server pages in a WKWebView, and those are authenticated by COOKIE — `getServerSession()` reads the session store and never consults the header. A WKWebView cannot attach an `Authorization` header to a top-level navigation, and the system-browser flow writes its cookies into Safari’s jar rather than the app’s. So after a flawless native sign-in the bearer is valid and the webview is still logged out; this closes that gap. 

Call it with the bearer in the `Authorization` header, then follow the redirect: the response sets the session cookie and sends the shell on to `next`. 

`next` is sanitised to a path within this origin — an open redirect here would be reached with a VALID credential, which is exactly when one is worth most to an attacker. 

**401 `invalid_bearer`** for an absent, malformed or revoked token.

schema.description: Same-origin path to land on. Sanitised server-side.

parameters.description: Same-origin path to land on. Sanitised server-side.
parameters.name: next

303.description: Sets the session cookie and redirects to `next`. No body.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: `invalid_bearer` — a BARE body, not the envelope.

403.description:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. They are tracked on #1677.

If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

post.summary: Spend a refresh token for a new pair
post.description:
Step 5 of the flow above, and the reason the sign-in handshake only has to happen once. Send `{ "refreshToken": "…" }`; the answer is a COMPLETE new pair and the token sent is consumed. Rotation is unconditional — there is no "still valid, reuse it" reply — so a client must persist the new `refreshToken` before discarding the old one, or it has locked itself out. 

Unauthenticated by construction: the refresh token IS the credential, which puts this in the same abuse position as sign-in and is why it is rate-limited at the pre-auth tier rather than the default one. Do not send an `Authorization` header expecting it to matter — an expired access token is the normal reason to be here. 

This route FAILS CLOSED, unlike per-request bearer verification: the underlying session is re-checked live and a revoked or expired one is refused. That is the moment a native client actually loses access after an admin revokes it. 

The new access token is rebuilt from the session’s CURRENT claims, never from anything the client sent, so a changed role, a lost membership or a deleted tenant is reflected in the next access token. A refresh is not a way to keep stale authority alive, and a client must not assume its claims survive one unchanged. 

**Every failure is `401 { "error": "invalid_grant" }`** — malformed body, unknown token, revoked session and a REPLAYED token are indistinguishable on purpose (see the module docblock). Note this is 401 where `/exchange` uses 400 for the same shape. The only correct client response to either is to discard the pair and restart at `/api/auth/native/start`.

401.description: `invalid_grant` — a BARE body, as RFC 6749 §5.2 specifies. Covers an unknown, expired, rotated or revoked refresh token, deliberately indistinguishable.

post.summary: Begin registration: create an unverified account and email a 6-digit code
post.description:
Step 1 of registration v2. Creates an account whose email is NOT yet verified and emails a 6-digit code. It creates no farm — the email is proven first, and the farm is created afterwards by `POST /api/me/farms`.

**Every outcome returns the same 200 body.** A new address, an address part-way through signing up, and an address that already has a full account are indistinguishable in the response — deliberately, because the route it replaces answered `409 Email already registered` and was therefore a working account-enumeration oracle. The difference lands in the mailbox instead: a code for the first two cases, a "you already have an account" notice for the third. So a client must NOT infer anything about the address from a success, and must not tell the user "account created" — the honest message is "check your email".

The password is hashed on every path, including the ones that discard it, so the request takes the same time whether or not the address is known. A client that times this endpoint learns nothing.

An existing password is never overwritten by this call. Calling it again for an address that is already part-way through signing up reissues the CODE only.

400 means the REQUEST was wrong — a malformed body, a password failing policy, a password found in a breach corpus, or a refused Turnstile challenge (`turnstile_failed`, carrying Cloudflare error codes so a client can reset the widget; a token is single-use, so a blind retry always fails). Those say nothing about any address, which is why they are distinguishable from the uniform 200.

Since P3.1 two further 400s join that list, and for the same reason — both are statements about the REQUEST, not the address: `terms_not_accepted` when consent is absent or not literally `true`, and `terms_version_stale` when the client names a version other than the one being served, carrying `currentVersion` so the client can reload and show the new terms rather than a generic failure.

get.summary: The terms version to send back, and where to read them
get.description:
Read this BEFORE `POST /api/auth/accept-terms`, which requires `termsVersion` to equal the version the server is serving. Until this route existed, nothing told a non-browser client what that value was — the web renders `/terms` itself so it has the constant in hand, and a native client did not (agrent-ios P4.4).

**It is the way out of a trap, not a convenience.** A first Sign in with Apple answers `termsPending: true`, after which every `/api/t/**` and `/api/me/**` is a 403 until acceptance is recorded. A client that cannot learn the version is held there permanently, and for an Apple-only account using Hide My Email there is no web fallback.

**Public and ungated**, like the document itself: an anonymous reader and a signed-in one see the same version. It is under `/api/auth/` so a `termsPending` session can reach it — that session is the one which MUST be able to.

**Do not cache across sessions.** The version changes when the terms change, which is exactly when a stale read is harmful: you would send a version the user did not see.

On `400 terms_version_stale` from accept-terms, re-read this, show the document again and ask again. **Never retry with the `currentVersion` the error carries** — that files consent against a version the user never read, which is worse than the error, because the stored row is the only legal artifact the product keeps.

200.description: The current terms version and the page to read.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. post.summary: Validate an ЕИК with the value in the request BODY (preferred)
post.description:
Identical to the GET in every respect but one: the number travels in the body rather than the query string. **Prefer this method.**

**Why it exists.** Every request to this endpoint is potentially an ЕГН — a personal identity number — because that is what the endpoint is for: a sole trader reaching for "the number I know" types theirs into the ЕИК box, which is exactly what `looksLikeEgn` detects. A query string is logged in places a body is not: iOS CFNetwork records the full request URL unsuppressably, and a GET URL also reaches browser history and can leak through `Referer`. The server side is clean (no access log, and the request logger uses the path only), so this is a CLIENT-side exposure — which makes it no less real for the person whose device is doing the logging.

**There is no GET form.** One existed until #1356 and was removed: the number travelled in the query string, which iOS CFNetwork records in full, unsuppressably. If you are holding a client that calls it, send the same value in a body instead — the response is byte-for-byte identical.

Rate-limited rather than hidden: unauthenticated, so there is no credential to scope an answer to. Expect 429 under load and back off; do not retry tightly.

- `SEASON_INVALID_DATE` — a supplied `startDate` or `endDate` is not a date. `params.field` names which, comma-joined when both are bad, the same shape create uses.

Rows already holding an inverted window are left alone and stay readable — they are not migrated.

post.description:
Creates the PLAN only. No plantings exist until `POST /crop-plans/{id}/generate` is called — `_count.plantings` of 0 is the tell.

**Refusal codes.**
- `CROP_PLAN_NAME_REQUIRED` — the name was blank or sanitised to nothing.

- `INVALID_SEASON`, `INVALID_CROP_TYPE`, `INVALID_VARIETY`, `INVALID_PARCEL` — the referenced id does not resolve in this farm. All four are resolved through the tenant-bound session, so another farm’s id and a non-existent one are deliberately indistinguishable.
- `PARCEL_LOCATION_MISMATCH` — the parcel resolves, but it does not belong to the location also given. Separate from `INVALID_PARCEL` because both ids are individually valid and it is the PAIR that is wrong.

post.description:
Materialises the succession pattern into PLANTINGS — `successions` rows spaced `intervalDays` apart from `firstSowDate`. This is the only way plantings come into existence; there is no create-planting route. 

Read `_count.plantings` on the plan before calling if you need to know whether it has already been generated.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

THREE PERMISSION codes are described here, and they are the most diffuse of all of them — 106, 51 and 1 call sites respectively, under most mutating and administrative operations in this document:

The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`.
