400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. - `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

get.summary: Trace a lot’s provenance both ways
get.description:
The FOOD-SAFETY RECALL query. Walks the genealogy graph up to the seed and input lots this one derives from, and down to the harvest lots derived from it, annotating every node with the fields it touched. 

"Given this seed lot, which fields and which harvest lots are implicated?" — and its inverse, "given this harvest, what went into it?". `edges` carries the parent/child links so a client can draw the graph rather than infer it from the arrays.

get.summary: NDVI tile source for a location
get.description:
A recent cloud-masked Sentinel-2 NDVI composite for the location’s field, via Google Earth Engine, Redis-cached. 

Returns JSON, not imagery — `tileUrl` is what a map layer then fetches. 

Handle all THREE states: `configured:false` (no credentials — show a muted hint, not an error), `configured:true` with an EMPTY `tileUrl` (nothing to show; keep the map, leave the overlay off), and a real URL. 

**Display the returned `date`, not the one you asked for** — the composite falls back to the latest available window, so they legitimately differ. 

Reachable by the restricted MECHANISATOR persona, which is deliberate: the sprayer needs the map on the job.

404.description:

post.description:
PUBLIC and session-less — the `token` in the body IS the credential, and the tenant is resolved from the stream it matches. Device-facing. 

**Every rejection is the SAME vague 401** `{ "error": "access_denied" }` — unknown stream, wrong token and disabled stream are indistinguishable on purpose, so probing stream ids gives no oracle. Do not branch on the reason. 

**503 `{ "error": "feature_disabled" }`** when the operator has not enabled the feature; that is a deployment state, not a client error, and retrying will not change it. 

This route deliberately does NOT use the standard error envelope — these bare `{ error }` shapes are its contract, which is why its failures look unlike the rest of this API.

200.description: Accepted. `inserted` is how many rows landed.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

THREE PERMISSION codes are described here, and they are the most diffuse of all of them — 106, 51 and 1 call sites respectively, under most mutating and administrative operations in this document:

- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not modify records. Params: `role`. It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

delete.description:
Answers with the id only.

Refusal code: `LEASE_NOT_FOUND` (404).

Newest settlement first.

Raises NO lease-specific refusal, and that is worth knowing rather than discovering: an unknown `leaseId` returns an EMPTY ARRAY, not a 404. So a client cannot tell "this lease has no payments" from "there is no such lease" on this operation, and must not render the empty case as proof the lease exists. It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

Retry-After.description: Whole seconds to wait before retrying. `max(1, ceil(retryAfterMs / 1000))`, so it is never 0 — a client that retries immediately on 0 would spend the next window the moment it opens. The same number is in the body as `retryAfterSeconds`.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: The preset ceiling for this scope, in requests per window.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

get.description:
The season’s totals. `seasonName` is NULL when the recap is all-time rather than scoped to a season — that is a mode, not a missing name. 

Read `totalYieldTonnes` and `totalNetTonnesStd` as different things: the first is GROSS, the second is moisture-standardised, and `recordsWithMoisture` says how many records could be standardised at all. `costPerHa` is null when NO row carried a cost, which is different from a cost of zero.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

post.description:
POST because generating the document is a job with a body, not a lookup. Returns PDF BYTES with `Content-Disposition` — do not attempt to decode JSON from it.

**A season with nothing recorded gets NO document** (#2183, owner ruling 2026-10-23): `404 REGISTER_EMPTY_FOR_PERIOD`, the same code the per-block register uses. A location whose own register is empty is skipped rather than contributing a lone cover page.

This replaced a fallback that composed up to 25 locations as blank ruled tables so the file was "a usable blank ДНЕВНИК" — which stopped being true once empty sections began to be omitted, because the result was 25 cover pages.

post.summary: Generate the whole-farm campaign ДНЕВНИК PDF
post.description:
The owner’s «ДНЕВНИК НА СТОПАНСТВОТО» (#2316) — the WHOLE FARM, every recorded activity, one landscape table of nine columns under seven headers. It REPLACES the БАБХ period download; the БАБХ register itself stays per treatment and is `/reports/season-diary` and the per-location routes.

**A row is an ACTIVITY, not a line.** «Пръскане – 17,05 ха» is one row for one spraying across several parcels — the sum of the parcels actually treated, in ХЕКТАРИ. The per-block register prints one row per parcel line instead.

**The campaign is DERIVED from the parameter, not a stored row.** `campaign=2024-2025` means 1 Oct 2024 → 30 Sep 2025, bounded in the farm’s own timezone with an EXCLUSIVE upper bound. `Season` can express that window, but production has exactly one Season, it is the sample dataset, and its window is 1 Mar – 31 Oct — so a picker backed by Season rows would offer one sample season with the wrong dates and an empty list on a tenant with none.

**Rows are not capped.** The per-block register caps field SHEETS but deliberately not lines, because a vanished spray is an unrecorded chemical application; a campaign row is the same kind of record. A farm with years of history can therefore request a large document.

schema.description: The campaign, `YYYY-YYYY`.

parameters.description: The campaign, `YYYY-YYYY`.
parameters.name: campaign

400.description: - a malformed `campaign` — it must be `YYYY-YYYY` with CONSECUTIVE years. `2025-2024` and `2024-2026` are both parseable and neither is a campaign.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

Four of these come from `src/middleware.ts` rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on EVERY route and are the ones worth switching on:

- `ADMIN_REQUIRED` — the route is admin-only and this role is not.
- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Route-level 403s carry their own codes and are described on the operation that returns them.

One route-level code is described HERE rather than per-operation. MOST operations cannot return it — it is confined to the five capability families named below — but it means the same thing on each of them, and one of the five (`upload`) is gated at a choke point that many unrelated routes reach, so an exhaustive per-operation list would be the kind that is wrong by omission:

- `ACCOUNT_DELETION_PENDING` — this person asked to delete their account and is inside the 30-day grace period, so the account creates nothing new. It is NOT a moderator action and NOT a permission problem: do not offer an appeal. Reachable on any MUTATION outside `/api/auth/**` and `/api/account/**`, which stay open precisely so the way out stays open — `DELETE /api/account/deletion` cancels it, and the person recovers their account and their listings in full. Reads are unaffected, and `GET /api/account/export` keeps working, because a right of access does not lapse because a right of erasure was invoked.

- `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` — a payment on this tenant failed and the 14-day grace period has elapsed. It is NOT a quota or a plan ceiling: the plan is untouched and nothing was exceeded. The withheld capabilities are exactly `exchange`, `trends`, `task.create`, `upload` and `journal.create`; every other surface, including reading everything already recorded, is unaffected. The tenant's own ACTIVE exchange listings stay visible to other farms and inbound threads keep arriving — this is the unpaid tenant's own view closing, not a withdrawal.

  The restriction is COMPUTED per request, with no sweep and nothing to settle, so a cleared balance lifts it on the very next request — a client can honestly tell the user to resolve it and refresh. This description deliberately names no remedy beyond that: App Store guideline 3.1.1 keeps the native client from pointing anyone to pay outside the app, so a prescribed destination would be unreachable for one of the two clients (#1490). What both clients CAN do is distinguish this from `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` and say which happened.

Five billing and capability codes are described here for the same reason and with the same caveat: each is confined to the routes that reach one gate, those gates sit below many operations, and an exhaustive per-operation list would be wrong by omission. Each carries `params` so a client composes its own sentence rather than rendering ours (#1679):

- `PLAN_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — a per-plan ceiling on a COUNT was reached. Params: `plan`, `resource`, `limit`, `current`. Reachable wherever `assertWithinLimit` guards a create. It is NOT a payment problem and NOT a permission shortfall: nothing failed and no role lifts it. The remedy is a higher plan or deleting something, and this description names no destination for the same reason `PAST_DUE_RESTRICTED` does not.
- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. It resets at the start of the next **UTC** month with nothing to settle, so a client can honestly say "next month" — which is what distinguishes it from the one above, where waiting changes nothing. UTC is stated because it is not local: for a Bulgarian user the reset lands at 02:00 or 03:00 on the 1st (EET/EEST), so copy naming a DAY would be wrong for a few hours each month. Raised by agrent-ios, which got this right before the spec said it.
- `AI_TIER_NOT_ALLOWED` — the requested model TIER is above this plan's ceiling. Params: `plan`, `tier`, `ceiling`. Distinct from the budget code on purpose: the refusal is on capability, not on spend, so retrying at `ceiling` succeeds immediately and retrying the same tier never will.
- `MODULE_DISABLED` — a product module is off for this tenant. Params: `module` and `reason`. AVAILABLE is a conjunction (plan-allowed AND tenant-enabled) and `reason` says which half failed, because the remedies differ: `"tenant"` means an administrator of THIS farm can turn it on, `"plan"` means the plan does not include it and no administrator can. Do NOT name an administrator without reading `reason` — telling somebody to ask an admin who cannot help is the defect agrent-ios#241 is about, and an earlier draft of this paragraph said exactly that. A client that ignores `reason` should stay neutral; the code alone only means "off".
- `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — this deployment runs self-hosted and exposes no in-app checkout at all. Params: `mode`. Nothing the client or the user can do lifts it; do not offer a retry or a plan picker.

  TWO of the five are TRANSLATED by the server (#1677) — `MODULE_DISABLED` and `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE` — so their `message` is renderable to a user. The other three still carry an English developer-facing sentence: their Bulgarian needs ICU plural agreement, which the server-side renderer does not yet do, and shipping copy that interpolated a wire identifier (`exchange_listing`, `deep`, `FREE`) into a farmer's screen would have been worse than the English. They are tracked on #1677.

  All five carried a legacy `lower_snake:` prefix at the start of `message` until #1677; that prefix is GONE for all of them. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec and your client matches on `plan_limit_exceeded:` or a sibling, switch to `code` — the prefix was removed once the only client depending on it had shipped the codes.

THREE PERMISSION codes are described here, and they are the most diffuse of all of them — 106, 51 and 1 call sites respectively, under most mutating and administrative operations in this document:

- `WRITE_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not modify records. Params: `role`. It refuses exactly three of the six roles — READER, MECHANISATOR and AUDITOR — and no other condition produces it: it is NOT a plan ceiling, NOT a payment problem, and NOT a moderator action, so retrying, paying or waiting all change nothing. The remedy is a different role, which only an administrator of that farm can grant, and `params.role` is there so a client can name the role the person actually holds rather than guessing.

  Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only. This one comes from a usecase and means the OPERATION needs write. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this.

  Uncoded until #1767, which is why a client reading a cached copy of this spec should treat its absence as "this server predates the code" rather than "this server cannot refuse a write".

- `ADMIN_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role in THIS farm may not perform this ADMINISTRATIVE action. Params: `role`. 51 call sites, and it refuses four of the six roles — EDITOR, AUDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR.

  **Distinguish it from `ADMIN_REQUIRED` above, which is a different condition and not a variant of this one.** That one comes from the Edge and means the ROUTE is admin-only: the whole area is closed to this role. This one comes from a usecase and means the route is NOT admin-only — the caller reached the handler legitimately — and this particular OPERATION needs admin. A role can pass the Edge and still meet this check, so a client that shows one sentence for both will tell an EDITOR they lack access to a screen they are looking at.

  Uncoded until #1779. `ADMIN_REQUIRED` was deliberately NOT renamed to make room for it: that code is one of the four reachable on every route and the most likely of all of them to be live in a shipped client, and a clearer name is not worth a breaking change to it.

- `AUDIT_FORBIDDEN_FOR_ROLE` — the caller's role may not perform AUDIT actions. Params: `role`. ONE call site, refusing EDITOR, READER and MECHANISATOR. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. No tenant route can answer either. They are here because that one function is the choke point all of those routes reach and three of their paths are not in this document yet, so a per-operation list would be wrong by omission:

- `API_KEY_NOT_PERSON_SCOPED` — an `iflk_` API key was presented on a route about a PERSON. A key belongs to a farm and authorises nobody in particular, so this is a category error rather than a permission shortfall: retrying with a wider-scoped key cannot work. Use a user session or a bearer token minted for one.
- `OPERATOR_SCOPE` — the signed-in user is a MECHANISATOR and the route is a social surface. Deliberately narrower than the Edge lockdown of the same persona: an operator reaches their own account and security pages normally, because a lockdown that locks somebody out of their own credentials is a defect (owner ruling, 2026-10-02). Nothing the client can do lifts it; do not offer a retry.

Both carried their code in `error.message` with a generic `error.code` until #1645. If you are reading a cached copy of this spec, check that it carries this sentence before switching on either.

404.description: - `REGISTER_EMPTY_FOR_PERIOD` — the campaign recorded nothing, or recorded only incomplete work. Not a fault; say so rather than showing an error, and note that a 200 with an empty table would be indistinguishable from a genuinely quiet period.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: Always `0` on a 429 — present for symmetry with the other headers.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: Unix time in SECONDS at which the window frees up.

404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

Two codes here come from the TENANT RESOLVER rather than from any handler, so they are reachable on every `/api/t/**` route and are the ones worth switching on (#1712):

- `TENANT_NOT_FOUND` — no such farm, OR a farm this caller may not see, OR one removed from the organisation. The three are DELIBERATELY indistinguishable and share one code: a response that told them apart would let a caller enumerate farms by slug. So do not offer "check the address" as though the farm were certainly absent — the honest message is that it is not available to this account.
- `TENANT_IDENTIFIER_REQUIRED` — the request reached the resolver with neither a slug nor an id. In practice this means a session carrying no tenant, so re-authenticating or picking a farm is the way out rather than retrying. The 404 status is historical and kept on purpose: changing it would break a client that already handles 404 here, and the #1712 migration is about the LANGUAGE a farmer reads.

Both carried an English sentence and no code until #1712. The iOS client resolves display from `error.message` and has no `NOT_FOUND` entry, so an uncoded 404 reached a Bulgarian farmer as English — which is the whole reason these are coded rather than merely translated.

200.description: The profile. `ETag` carries the version as a strong tag; `version` carries it in the body.

put.description:
Requires `admin.manage`. An upsert, so the first write creates the row. 

A BLANK STRING CLEARS a field — it is not ignored. An ABSENT field is left ALONE (see the body schema) — true since #1176, and this sentence previously said the opposite. 

The server normalises on write: text is trimmed and sanitised, a negative `sizeHa` is refused (stored as null), and `grainProduced` has blanks dropped and duplicates removed case-insensitively while PRESERVING ORDER. schema.description: The `version` you last read, as a BARE INTEGER (`5`) or a STRONG entity-tag (`"5"`) — both are accepted, and the `ETag` from GET round-trips verbatim. A WEAK tag (`W/"5"`) is REFUSED with a 400: RFC 7232 forbids weak comparison for If-Match and it is meaningless for a version lock. Anything else non-numeric is also a 400 rather than being ignored — unlike the journal and field-operations routes, which silently fall through to NO precondition on a header they cannot parse (#1182). OPTIONAL: omit it and the write is last-write-wins, exactly as before this lock existed. Omitting it is not an error and never will be without notice — an installed mobile build sends none. `If-Match: 0` means "the profile does not exist yet, create it": 0 is a sentinel no stored row carries, so it fails with a 409 if someone created the row first.

get.summary: The farms the caller belongs to
get.description:
Every farm the caller is an ACTIVE member of, for a farm switcher. Authenticated, no tenant context.

**Ordered by membership age, oldest first, and that is a contract rather than a convenience.** `farms[0]` is the same farm `GET /api/auth/me` names in its `tenant` field, so a client can reconcile this list against the farm it opens on a fresh install.

**Removed farms are excluded.** Soft-deleting a tenant sets only `deletedAt` and deliberately leaves memberships active, so a removed farm still has live memberships pointing at it — those are filtered here, as they are by the tenant picker, the JWT claims and the tenant resolver. A farm absent from this list is unreachable, not merely unlisted.

Not read from the JWT: `session.user.memberships` is capped at `MAX_JWT_MEMBERSHIPS` for cookie-size safety, and a switcher that silently dropped a farm past the cap would be worse than no switcher. This is a database read every time.

An empty array means the caller belongs to no farm — not an error. That is the state the registration wizard exists for.

200.description: The caller's farms, oldest membership first. Empty when they belong to none.

Do NOT render a success state implying the claim was accepted, and do not poll this endpoint for a verdict: the real state is readable only from inside the farm, where row-level security scopes it to the people who belong there.

**A second farm is not a conflict.** One person may hold several; expect no 409 on the second call.

get.summary: Новини — the signed-in reader’s own tag opt-ins
get.description:
Account-level, with no `{tenantSlug}`: a news preference is a property of the PERSON, not of a farm. put.summary: Новини — replace the signed-in reader’s tag opt-ins
put.description:
Replaces the stored list for the session user. 

**400s on a tag outside the catalogue, naming it** — deliberately the OPPOSITE of `?tags=` on the feed, which ignores unknown keys. The two answer different questions about who chose the value: a `PUT` is a person choosing, where a typo is a client bug worth surfacing, while the feed parameter is a pass-through of state the server itself issued and may since have renamed. Reject unknown on write, ignore unknown on read. 

The 400 carries `code: "INVALID_NEWS_PREFERENCES"`.

200.description: The stored list, as persisted. `tags` is never null here.

post.summary: Publish one event to your own realtime channel
post.description:
Publishes one event to the CALLING USER’S own channel and writes nothing. It exists so a synthetic probe can assert that a realtime event really arrives end to end (P7.9) — every other producer notifies somebody else, and task assignment is deliberately silent when the assignee is the actor, so there is no way to provoke an event for yourself through the product’s own surfaces. 

**You can only ping yourself.** The channel is built from your own session, so no parameter names a recipient. The worst outcome is that your own tabs refetch your own notification list. 

**No `Notification` row is created**, so this cannot put text in front of anybody, including you. A client that receives the id refetches and finds nothing new — which is the correct outcome, because the assertion is about the transport. 

**Deliberately NOT gated on `notifications.sse`.** With the flag off, a gated endpoint would refuse here AND the stream would answer 204, leaving a probe unable to tell "off by decision" from "the publisher is broken". Publishing is always allowed; whether anybody is listening is the stream’s business. 

The id is prefixed `probe-` and is deliberately not cuid-shaped, so it can never be mistaken for a `Last-Event-ID` replay cursor.

get.description:

**Every event carries an SSE `id:` line**, and that is what makes reconnect cheap: `EventSource` echoes the last one back as `Last-Event-ID`, and this route answers it by replaying up to 50 ids created after that cursor, oldest first. Send the header yourself if you are not using `EventSource`. A client that receives nothing on reconnect — an unknown cursor, or one older than it can resolve — should simply refetch its list, which is what it does on a cold open. 

**At most 3 concurrent streams per person**, counted in Redis across processes. The fourth is refused rather than evicting an older one, because eviction would close a live tab and that tab would reconnect. 

**A 204 means "do not reconnect"** and has three causes a client cannot distinguish: realtime is disabled for the deployment, the session has no trackable lineage, or the person is already at three streams. Per the `EventSource` specification a non-200 fails the connection without a reconnect, which is the intent in all three cases. 

**The session is re-checked every 5 minutes** and the stream is CLOSED on a revoked one, rather than going quiet — a silent stream is indistinguishable from an idle one, so closing is what lets the client discover it is signed out on its own reconnect. 

**Every farm on one connection.** The stream carries events from every farm the caller belongs to, and each frame names its own `tenantId` — so one connection serves somebody in three farms rather than needing three. Delivery was scoped to the active farm until the frame could name the tenant (#2085). The stream is ONE-WAY. 

**`id:` lines accompany `notification` frames only.** It is the replay cursor and replay reads the `Notification` table, so a `listing` frame advances no cursor — exchange events are live-only, and a reconnecting client refetches Борса over REST with ETag, which is what it does on a cold open. 

It does NOT replace `GET /api/notifications/stream`, which is live and carries whole notifications; the two coexist until the web hook (P7.6) and the iOS client (P7.7) move across.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:

post.summary: DSA Art 16 — file a notice without an account
post.description:
The anonymous notice mechanism. Art 16 requires a way for **any** person or entity to notify illegal content, so requiring an account would be requiring an account to exercise a right — this is the one write path in the product that accepts a body from nobody. 

**It is not behind a feature flag**, and that is a duty rather than an oversight: a legal obligation cannot be dark-launched, because a flag defaulting OFF means the obligation is unmet until someone remembers to flip it. 

**Nothing identifying is stored.** No IP, no hash of one, no surrogate. Rate limiting is the control instead, at 10/min per IP — tightened from the 60/min a public mutation gets by default, because the harm here is a flood that buries real notices in the triage queue rather than database load. The limiter sees the IP; the row never does. 

Send `reporterUserId` and it is silently dropped, not rejected: a caller can neither attribute a notice to someone else nor learn from an error whether the field exists.

The person BLOCK routes are a product feature and ARE gated — that difference is deliberate.

get.summary: DSA Art 16 — the notices you filed, and what became of them
get.description:
Newest first, capped at 100. Account-level with no `{tenantSlug}`: a notice is a property of the PERSON and carries no tenant, and a tenant-scoped route could not serve this at all — the policy that admits a reporter matches a session variable only the person-scoped runner sets, so under a tenant context it would return zero rows with no error, indistinguishable from having filed none.

post.description:
Refuses further contact from that person, person-to-person. ADDITIONAL to the exchange block, which is a farm refusing a person; collapsing the two would silently un-block everyone already blocked on the exchange.

The effect is SILENT on the enforcement side: the blocked person is never told. An exchange conversation between the two disappears from THEIR view — read, list and send all answer the same not-found a genuinely missing thread does — while the blocker keeps full history. Blocking yourself is refused with `BLOCK_SELF`.

Idempotent: blocking twice is one row and answers 200 with `alreadyBlocked: true`.

**Gated on `social.person-blocks`** and 404s while that flag is off. Unlike the notice routes above, which are a legal duty and cannot be dark-launched, blocking is a product feature (and an Apple 1.2 requirement).

The person id travels in the BODY, including on `DELETE`. That is unusual and deliberate: iOS logs the full request URL including the path, unsuppressably, so a third party's user id in a path would end up in a device log — the exact disclosure this phase exists to prevent.

Removes the caller's own block.

post.summary: Moderation — record a decision on a notice

`actionKind: "NONE"` is a real outcome, not a no-op: "looked and did nothing" must be distinguishable from "never looked", and it moves the notice to REJECTED — the judgement.

**The moderator is taken from the verified key and is never read from the body.** It records which key GENERATION authorised the action (current or previous), which narrows a compromise window to one side of a rotation. It is deliberately **not a person**: there is one platform key for every operator, so a regulator asking "who decided this" gets "somebody holding the key". Per-moderator attribution needs per-moderator credentials — tracked in P5.8.

The subject is denormalised from the notice, so an action cannot be recorded against content it was not about. `rationale` is REQUIRED — unlike a notice’s `detail`, because a decision without a reason is what Art 17 exists to prevent, and it is the text the statement is built from.

404 when the notice does not exist. Unlike the public notice route, a platform admin is entitled to that difference — there it would be an enumeration oracle.

get.description:
Art 17 statements written and not yet sent, oldest first.

**This is the drain queue, and surfacing it is part of the duty.** A statement that never went out is a compliance failure, and what makes it dangerous is that nothing else would show it: the action is recorded, the notice reads ACTIONED, and the recipient simply never heard. The lag from `createdAt` to `deliveredAt` is also how P5’s median-handling criterion is measured rather than asserted.

`bodyRendered` is NOT returned. It is the delivered text, encrypted at rest, and this view needs to know THAT something is stuck rather than to re-read what it says.

**Platform-admin key**, not a tenant permission. Every role in the enum is tenant-scoped, so `admin.manage` would let an ADMIN of any one farm read every other farm’s notices — which is also why the underlying tables deny `app_user` outright rather than relying on this route to filter.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

403.description:
Signed in, but not permitted.

- `CSRF_BLOCKED` — a cross-site admin request. Retrying will not help; the request must originate from the app.
- `MFA_REQUIRED` — the session carries a pending MFA challenge. Complete it and retry; the credential is valid.
- `TERMS_ACCEPTANCE_REQUIRED` — consent has not been recorded. `POST /api/auth/accept-terms` is the way out, and the session must be re-minted afterwards because `termsPending` is a JWT claim.

Each carries a `message`. Since #1677 the SERVER translates it, into the language on the signed-in person's profile (`User.uiLanguage`, default Bulgarian) — NOT negotiated from `Accept-Language`, which this API deliberately ignores. So `message` is safe to render to a user for any code that has a catalogue entry.

  The migration is INCOMPLETE and visibly so: a code with no entry yet keeps its English developer-facing sentence, unchanged. There is no flag telling the two apart, which is why switching on `code` and holding your own copy remains the robust choice — the server's `message` is then a better fallback than it used to be rather than something you depend on. Coded in the same change as its sibling rather than on its own merits: three sibling helpers raising two coded refusals and one bare string is the state that invites a reader to assume the bare one is deliberate.

Two more are described here rather than per-operation, and their scope is NARROWER than the four above: they come from `getUserCtx`, so they are reachable on the PERSON-scoped routes only — `/api/account/**`, `/api/me/**` and `/api/social/**`. 404.description:
Not found, or not visible to this tenant.

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

delete.description:
Restores access on the next request. This is the DSA redress path: a suspension with no way back is a permanent ban wearing a temporary name.

**Platform-admin key**, not a tenant permission. Every role in the enum is tenant-scoped, so `admin.manage` would let an ADMIN of any one farm read every other farm’s notices — which is also why the underlying tables deny `app_user` outright rather than relying on this route to filter.

wasSuspended.description: False when the account was not suspended — the call is idempotent rather than an error.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

get.summary: Everyone with a membership in this farm
get.description:
**Not a roster.** Returns `ACTIVE`, `INVITED` and `DEACTIVATED` memberships, so `status` is load-bearing: a client rendering this as "current staff" shows deactivated people with no indication. That inclusion is INTENDED and at least one client relies on it — grouping by status, offering reactivation on a deactivated row, and counting every row so its displayed total matches the list behind it.

**`REMOVED` is excluded.** `DELETE …/{membershipId}` sets that status precisely so the row leaves this list, so "removed" is an absence here and never a value to display. A UI group for it can never fill.

Ordered by `createdAt` ASCENDING — oldest membership first, so the owner tends to be row one. That is the opposite of the invite list, which is newest-first.

**`?view=invites` returns the PENDING INVITE list instead**, byte-identical to `GET /admin/invites`. It is the same usecase and the same response; neither path is deprecated and a change to one would need the other. Prefer `/admin/invites`, which says what it returns.

For a list of people to assign work to, use the assignable-users endpoint rather than this one: it is `ACTIVE`-only, carries no session counts, and is readable by any signed-in member instead of admins alone.

schema.description: The ONLY accepted value, and it changes the response TYPE to the pending-invite list. Any other value — or none — returns members. There is no `view=members`.

parameters.description: The ONLY accepted value, and it changes the response TYPE to the pending-invite list. Any other value — or none — returns members. There is no `view=members`.
parameters.name: view

200.description: The farm's memberships, oldest first. With `?view=invites`, the pending-invite array instead.

- `AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` — the tenant has spent its monthly AI token budget. Params: `plan`, `limit`, `used`. 404.description:

426.description: Client too old — the declared `x-agrent-client-version` is below the supported floor. The request was not processed; it is NOT a payload rejection.

post.description:
**Creates an INVITE, not a membership.** Nobody joins until they accept, so a 201 here does not add a row to `GET /admin/members` as ACTIVE — it adds one to the pending-invite list.

**Identical to `POST /admin/invites`**: same body, same usecase, same email, same response. This is the path the web admin UI calls. They share ONE 20/hr rate-limit budget keyed per tenant, so twenty invites through either door in an hour exhausts both — handle 429 with `Retry-After` on both.

**`emailSent: false` is a real outcome of a 201.** The invite is committed before the mail is attempted and a mailer failure never fails creation. Show the admin `url` to pass on by hand rather than reporting a failure, and never retry the POST on it — that mints a second invite.

`MECHANISATOR` is assignable here, and is deliberately absent from the roles an SSO/SCIM provisioning run may assign. Do not infer the provisionable set from this enum; the two disagree by design.

201.description: The invite exists. Check `emailSent` before telling the admin the person was notified.

400.description: Invalid request body or query parameters.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

patch.description:
Both fields are optional and they are applied INDEPENDENTLY — `role` sets the enum role, `customRoleId` assigns or (when `null`) unassigns a custom role.

**Sending both in one request is accepted, and the RESPONSE then describes the custom-role assignment rather than the role change.** The handler applies them in sequence and returns the result of whichever ran last. Send one field per request if you need the response to describe the change you made.

**Sending neither is a 400**, coded `NO_CHANGES_SPECIFIED`.

That sentence previously read "the error body is not the standard `ErrorResponse` envelope" — which documented a defect instead of fixing it, on an operation whose 400 this same document declares AS `ErrorResponse`. Two adjacent fields of one spec contradicting each other is worse than either alone, so the route was corrected rather than the sentence softened (#1447).

Refusals that live in the usecase rather than the route: promoting or demoting yourself, and removing the role from the last active OWNER/ADMIN. A farm must never become unadministrable.

**Refusal code.** `MEMBERSHIP_NOT_FOUND` — one code for every membership lookup on this surface, with `params.requiredStatus` naming the state the operation needed. Four codes would advertise a distinction the SERVER CANNOT MAKE: each of these is a single query with a status predicate, so an absent membership and one in the wrong state both come back empty. The English message says which wording applies; the param says which state was required. Here `requiredStatus` is `ACTIVE`: a deactivated member’s role is not editable, and a client should refresh rather than retry.

delete.summary: Remove a membership from the farm
delete.description:
**The hard one.** Sets `REMOVED`, which makes the row leave `GET /admin/members` entirely — there is no state to display afterwards and no documented route back. For a reversible action use `POST …/{membershipId}/deactivate`, which keeps the row listed as `DEACTIVATED` and has a `reactivate` counterpart.

Self-removal and removing the last active OWNER/ADMIN are refused in the usecase, so a farm cannot be left unadministrable.

Note the asymmetry with the bulk paths: `bulk/remove` is the bulk form of THIS operation, while `bulk/delete` is the bulk form of `deactivate`.

Four codes would advertise a distinction the SERVER CANNOT MAKE: each is a single query with a status predicate, so an absent membership and one in the wrong state both come back empty. Here `requiredStatus` is `ACTIVE,DEACTIVATED,INVITED` — anything but already-removed. So this refusal usually means somebody else removed them first, and a client should refresh rather than retry: the outcome it wanted has already happened.

401.description: Not signed in, or the session was refused.

post.summary: Deactivate several memberships (the path name says delete)

get.description:
Newest first — the opposite order to the members list.

**An invite leaves this list for three different reasons and all three look identical.** The filter is `acceptedAt: null` AND `revokedAt: null` AND `expiresAt > now`, so accepted, withdrawn and EXPIRED invites are equally absent. There is no `expired` state to render, and "never invited" is the same observation as all three.

That makes the obvious client behaviour — offer to re-invite when someone is absent — correct in every case, while the obvious client COPY ("no pending invites") is misleading for an invite that quietly timed out after its seven days. If a visible expired state is wanted, it is a server change.

**Carries no acceptance token.** The token is a bearer credential valid until `expiresAt`; it is returned once, in the `url` of the create response (#1450). To send someone a fresh link, create a new invite.

`GET /admin/members?view=invites` returns this exact list from the same usecase. Prefer this path.

200.description: Pending invites, newest first. Empty when none are outstanding.

**Identical to `POST /admin/members`** — same body, same usecase, same email, same `201 { invite, url, emailSent }`. Neither is deprecated.

post.summary: Replace the ПРЗ register from an uploaded file
post.description:
Loads the БАБХ register of approved plant-protection products. Owner ruling 2026-10-20: an upload, not a scheduled fetch. We own neither the register’s format nor its URL, so a parser pointed at them can break overnight — and the failure is not an exception, it is WRONG DOSES rendered identically to right ones. A manual upload makes a refresh a deliberate act with a known date, which turns staleness from silent into visible.

**NOTHING READS THIS REGISTER.** The crop × product suggestion it was built for was retired by the owner on 2026-10-21, who chose to keep the loader and drop the suggestions (#2077, closed as not planned). This operation and its GET are the only consumers: one writes an import, the other tells the operator what is live. Still documented because the upload still works and an operator may still load the register.

**An import REPLACES; it never merges.** A property of the stored data, kept for whatever may one day read it: the latest completed import IS the register, and older ones are provenance only. Merging would let a row withdrawn in the newest file still match from an older one, which is the worst thing these tables can produce.

**Columns bind by HEADER TEXT, never by position**, through an alias table, and the header is searched for in the first ten rows so a title or an issuing-order reference above it is fine. A bg-BG Excel writes SEMICOLON-delimited CSV, so the delimiter is sniffed across those leading rows rather than taken from the first line. The decimal separator may be a comma (`0,15`), and the unit may live in the header (`Доза (мл/дка)`) with bare numbers in the cells.

**Doses are read from the START of the cell.** A single value stores as both bounds; `150-200` as a range; `до 200` as a maximum with NO minimum, because storing 200 as both would assert a floor the register does not give. A cell like `0,1 л/100 л вода` yields 0.1 with unit `л/100 л вода` — reading every number in it would take 100 as the range top, a thousandfold error that renders like a correct one.

**The 400s, and all of them refuse the WHOLE upload** rather than dropping rows. A national register is used as a unit, and a version with an arbitrary subset silently missing is worse than no new version — a miss reads as "no product is approved for this crop".

- **Unbindable columns** — the message names the headers found and every accepted spelling of each missing field. This is the one to expect when a new year’s file changes shape; it usually means an alias needs adding.
- **No rows** — the columns bound but produced nothing. Refused rather than stored, since an empty register is a statement about Bulgarian law that a blank spreadsheet is not entitled to make.
- **A cell over 300 characters, or over 60 pests in one row** — the realistic parser failure is binding a product or pest column to a notes or conditions-of-use column, where every row looks fine individually and the tell is their length.
- **Scanner refusals** — the bytes are scanned before the parser is pointed at them. Nothing is stored or served, but "never stored" is not "never parsed": they go through a ZIP reader and an XML parser in-process.

Gated on `admin.manage` **inside** `PLATFORM_TENANT_SLUG`, and the gate is asserted before the body is even read, so a caller from another tenant pays for neither a scan nor a parse. Both halves are load-bearing: `admin.manage` resolves from Role, so the OWNER of every farm holds it, and alone it would hand any farm the national register. The gate FAILS CLOSED — an unset slug means 404 for everyone, the owner included.

get.summary: Which register import is live, and whether it is whole
get.description:
Exists so an upload is verifiable without database access: it answers "what is live right now", which the POST response cannot once the operator has closed the terminal.

`storedEntries` is COUNTED from the table while `entryCount` is what the import recorded. The two agreeing is the evidence that the snapshot is whole; reporting only the stored figure would make the check circular.

Same gate as the upload, failing closed the same way.

200.description: The live import, or null, plus a count of imports that never completed.

put.summary: Publish the farm’s public profile, or withdraw it
put.description:
`PUT` because the body IS the desired state: sending the same value twice leaves the same result, which is what makes it safe to retry on a flaky connection. `published` has no default — a client that omits it is refused rather than publishing a farm by accident, because publication is the direction that is hard to take back.

Withdrawing DELETES the public row rather than flagging it, so `/f/{handle}` stops answering outright. A rename is handled in the same call: the profile appears at the new address and the old row is removed, which is why `removedHandle` comes back alongside `handle`.

**This operation does not make a farm findable by search engines.** The projection carries an `indexable` flag which is always `false` today and is deliberately left alone by a refresh, so a republish cannot change it. The control belongs to the editor (P6.6, #1815), because "publish my page" and "let search engines index it" are different decisions.

**Refusal codes.**
- `FARM_BRAND_NOT_FOUND` (404) — this farm has no brand record to publish. A farm that has never opened the editor is in this state, so a client should offer to create one rather than reporting an error.
- `FARM_BRAND_HANDLE_REQUIRED` — no public address has been chosen. `/f/{handle}` has no other key, so there is nowhere to serve the page from.
- `FARM_BRAND_DISPLAY_NAME_REQUIRED` — no public name. Structural rather than editorial: the projection’s `displayName` is NOT NULL, so a farm without one cannot be represented at all.
- `FARM_BRAND_CONSENT_REQUIRED` — no consent has been recorded. Publishing identifiable information about a real farm without a record that somebody agreed is refused, and the consent sheet that records it is P6.6’s.

All three publication refusals are fail-closed and apply only to `published: true`. A withdrawal never fails on them — a farm must always be able to take its page down, including one whose brand record has since become incomplete.
